"Starship V4 will be ~70m long, which is roughly a 40% length increase and allows >60% more propellant load," the SpaceX CEO said.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

As usual, SpaceX and its founder Elon Musk are thinking big.

The company recovered the upper stage of its Starship megarocket for the first time ever on Saturday (Nov. 14), plucking it out of the sky with the "chopstick" arms of its Texas launch tower.

It was a huge moment for SpaceX, bringing its vision of full and rapid rocket reuse much closer to reality. But Elon Musk isn't one to dwell on the past or rest on laurels, so he soon outlined an even more ambitious future for Starship.

"Starship V4 will be ~70m [230 feet] long, which is roughly a 40% length increase and allows >60% more propellant load," Musk said via X, the social media platform he owns, on Sunday evening (Nov. 15). "Engine count will be raised to 9, with 3 more Raptor-Vacuum engines added, and these will be higher-thrust V4 engines."

The current version of Starship — the one that launched Friday (Nov. 13) on the vehicle's 15th test flight — is the V3. It's the largest and most powerful rocket ever built, standing 408 feet (124 m) tall when fully stacked with its Super Heavy first stage and Ship upper stage.

V3's Ship is 171 feet (52 m) tall and features six of SpaceX's Raptor V3 engines. (The similarly reusable Super Heavy V3 booster is powered by 33 Raptors.) So, as Musk noted in his post, the V4 Ship will be quite an upgrade in size and power.

Starship Die Cast Rocket Model Was $47.99 Now $39.99 on Amazon.

Even if you can't see SpaceX's Starship in person, you can score a model of your own. Standing at 13.77 inches (35 cm), this is a 1:375 ratio of SpaceX's Starship as a desktop model. The materials here are alloy steel and it weighs just 225g.

To provide a little perspective about that vehicle's planned dimensions: The V4 Ship will be the same height as a fully stacked Falcon 9, SpaceX's workhorse two-stage rocket, and much broader: Ship is 30 feet (9 m) across, while the Falcon 9's payload fairing is 17.1 feet (5.2 m) wide.

This isn't the first we've heard about a V4 Starship. Back in August 2025, for example, Musk posted a graphic showing Starship's planned progression from the V2 to the V3 to the V4, which he said is expected to debut in 2027.

That slide pegs the future Starship's total height at 466 feet (142 m), 200 feet (61 m) of which would be Ship. But those numbers are out of date, Musk stressed in the post, saying that V4 is "probably closer to 150m height."

So, yeah: If all goes according to plan, the next Starship will be nearly 500 feet tall.

Starship V4 will be ~70m long, which is roughly a 40% length increase and allows >60% more propellant load. Engine count will be raised to 9, with 3 more Raptor-Vacuum engines added, and these will be higher thrust V4 engines.November 16, 2026

The original Starship Flight 15 mission plan called for a double chopsticks catch, with both Super Heavy and Ship coming back to the launch tower for recovery.

This would have been feasible, as the catches were scheduled a day apart: Super Heavy would land just 6.5 minutes after launch, while Ship would circle Earth for 22.5 hours, and deploy a batch of SpaceX's Starlink V3 internet satellites, before coming home. (Ship ended up delivering the satellites as planned.)

The twofer didn't happen, however; Super Heavy experienced a low-fuel alarm and diverted to a Gulf of Mexico splashdown on Friday as a result. But that wasn't a huge deal, as SpaceX had already pulled off Super Heavy catches on three previous Starship flights.

The Ship catch was unprecedented, because it's been a taller order. Ship returns to Earth from orbit, so it comes in faster and hotter. SpaceX hadn't even tried the maneuver before Flight 15, so executing it was a very big deal.

"That was the missing link," SpaceX's Dan Huot said during the company's Ship-landing webcast on Saturday. "We caught a Starship, and now everything changes."

#764. Lainey Wilson Looks So Different Without Signature Bell Bottoms & Hat

Lainey Wilson looked almost unrecognizable as she stepped out at the 2026 CMAs in Nashville Nov. 18 without her signature bell bottom pants and cowboy hat.

Lainey Wilson is stepping away from bell bottom country.

The “Heart Like a Truck” singer ditched her signature flare pants and Western hat for a classic Oscar de la Renta gown at the 2026 CMA Awards.

Wilson—who is serving as host for the evening’s festivities—looked stunning in a light yellow feathered gown, which featured a short train and a halter neckline. She kept her accessories simple for the Nov. 18 ceremony at the Bridgestone Arena in Nashville, only donning earrings and a few rings to finish off her simple look. (See all the stars at the show here.)

The 34-year-old—who is also nominated for Entertainer of the Year, Female Vocalist of the Year and Single of the Year for her hit “Somewhere Over Laredo”—has made no secret of her penchant for bell bottoms and a cowboy hat over the years, explaining that she was inspired to create her signature look after arriving in Nashville.

“I get to Nashville and I realized pretty quickly that as a female in this business, you have to do something that's a little outside of the box,” she shared during an interview with the Country Music Hall of Fame and Museum in April. “I wasn't gonna get away with wearing a ball cap and skinny jeans.”

The realization made her think back to her childhood, as she remembered the first pair of bell bottoms she got at the age of 9—which was also the year she wrote her first song.

“They were blue leopard print,” she recalled. “I remember putting them on as a child and just thinking—I just felt sassy. I felt like I could do anything.”

“If I still had those pants, I'd still be trying to fit in them ‘cause I felt good,” she quipped. "I felt just like I could take on the world. It was kind of like my superhero costume.”

And that superhero costume quickly became her signature, alongside the cowgirl hat that she started wearing in the late 2010s. In fact, the look has become so associated with the country star, that fans even dress up in their own version of the outfit at her shows.

“It's cool to look out into the crowd now and see everybody in their bell bottoms and their hats,” she shared. “It feels like a little bit of a movement and it just makes me happy.”

#763. The 3pm football blackout: Outdated or still relevant in 2026?

The 3pm blackout has existed in English football since the 1960s

After 60 years, is time finally running out on the 3pm blackout in football?

With pretty much every available television slot now exhausted, next year the Premier League and the EFL are set to hold serious discussions about its future.

There are concerns, especially within non-league football, that removing the blackout could have detrimental effects on attendances and finances.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham agrees, urging caution and suggesting the health of the football pyramid should come first.

But many Premier League fans feel they are short-changed, locked out of many of their team's fixtures just because they live in this country.

Go anywhere else in the world, and every single match is available live.

With streaming so prevalent, to some the blackout feels archaic.

Yet it is a complex situation, and many feel the depth of English football's pyramid is like nowhere else.

BBC Sport looks at the history of the blackout, why it is unique to British football and the arguments for and against keeping it.

It is the start of the 1964-65 season and the BBC launches a programme called Match of the Day.

Highlights of one match would be broadcast on BBC Two, a channel which at the time was only available in London.

Yet some clubs were concerned. Would fans still turn up to games?

Burnley chairman Bob Lord was the first owner to refuse to allow the cameras into Turf Moor. At the end of the season, several other clubs tried to block the renewal of the deal.

A compromise was reached and the BBC agreed not to reveal the televised Saturday match until all games had ended.

Shortly afterwards came the blackout for live matches.

Fast forward 20 years to 1987. With dwindling attendances across the European domestic leagues, partly influenced by crowd trouble, Uefa took up England's idea.

Article 48 was added to the Uefa Statutes.

Each country could designate a two-and-a-half-hour "transmission-free period", as long as at least 50% of matches in the top two leagues were taking place.

This was "designed to ensure that spectators are not deterred from attending local football matches of any kind and/or participating in matches at amateur and/or youth level".

Today, the situation has gone full circle. The only leagues that apply Article 48 are England, Scotland and Northern Ireland.

The reason for this is simpler than you might imagine.

No other major country qualifies for the blackout - because no other major country has a kick-off time that runs from the top flight and through the divisions.

It is a tradition that is unique to football in the United Kingdom.

Let's take Germany, often held up as an example of a country with excellent attendances despite not having a blackout.

This misses a key point. The Bundesliga has its own kick-off slot, 3:30pm on a Saturday, and no other division plays at the same time. The 2. Bundesliga, for instance, has a standard Saturday kick-off time of 1:30pm.

Could you imagine English football replicating this?

In Spain, it is rare for either of the top two divisions to have games that kick off simultaneously. Each match has its own slot, and is broadcast live.

In Italy, Serie A plays on a Sunday afternoon, and Serie B on a Saturday.

In France, Ligue 1 has Saturday night as its main time slot, Ligue 2 plays largely on a Friday night, and Ligue 3 on a Saturday lunchtime.

So there is no blackout, because the football calendar works in a completely different way.

Football fans give their thoughts on the Saturday 3pm TV blackout

The next television rights cycle presents a unique opportunity.

The deals for the Premier League, EFL and Scottish Premiership are all up for renewal in 2029-30.

There is the chance for all the top stakeholders to come together and agree to end the blackout.

Last year, Premier League chief executive Richard Masters said there were no plans to remove the blackout.

But this summer there was a clear shift in emphasis, with Masters admitting there would be talks with the EFL ahead of the renewal of TV rights.

Scottish football has gone first, with broadcasters invited to bid to show all matches live - and is open to those shown on a Saturday afternoon.

It will be another year before we discover what the Premier League and the EFL - which seriously considered ending the blackout three years ago - are prepared to offer to broadcasters.

So, why would the leagues need to offer up the Saturday 3pm slot to broadcasters? After all, the latest domestic Premier League deal was worth a record Â£6.7bn - an increase of 4%.

However, to achieve that figure, the Premier League had to make an additional 70 games available. In real terms, it means each live Premier League game is worth less than it was before.

Now every single game not shown at 3pm on a Saturday - and there are only 110 left - is on TV.

Could the Premier League need to offer more matches for the rights to keep their overall value?

If so there are two options: try to find more TV slots, or show games at 3pm on a Saturday.

Could the Women's Super League benefit too? It looked into playing a 3pm on a Saturday but could not find a way around the blackout.

Most of the competition's games are shown live already, with a greater concern being stadium availability and consistency of kick-off times.

There is a danger that the issue of the 3pm blackout is viewed only through the lens of Premier League and EFL television rights.

Tom Greatrex, the chair of the Football Supporters' Association, says there are attendances in non-league football that some top flights in Europe "would look at jealously".

"We have one of the strongest football pyramids in the world, with excellent matchday attendances deep into the non-league game," Greatrex said.

"The prime minister is right to point out the value of the blackout to clubs further down the pyramid, and to urge caution over the impact rushed change could have on the overall health of the game."

BBC Sport understands that senior executives at the National League, which has a long-term global streaming deal with DAZN, are steadfastly against the blackout ending.

It has serious reservations, shared by the vast majority of its 72 clubs, that attendances would be impacted.

Included in this is transient attendance from season ticket holders of league clubs, many of whom go to non-league football when their team is away from home, boosting receipts considerably.

The fear is this could be lost if all league games are streamed at 3pm.

Nick Boom, the chair of Northern Premier League side FC United of Manchester, worries that the issue is only viewed through the lens of top-flight football.

"Football doesn't begin and end with the Premier League," Boom told BBC Sport.

"Every Saturday, thousands of people turn out to support their local clubs.

"For many of those clubs, the income from people coming through the turnstiles, buying a pint or something to eat is what keeps them alive.

"The 3pm blackout isn't about nostalgia. It's about protecting something that matters."

Boom added that clubs in non-league football are huge community assets, and losing them would have an impact "well beyond 90 minutes on a Saturday".

Some clubs are more open-minded about what ending the blackout could mean for non-league football.

Others have changed the way they operate to get around it.

North West Counties League Premier Division side FC Isle of Man have stopped playing at 3:00pm on a Saturday so they can stream all their games live.

Brian Shotton, a director at eighth-tier Ashington FC, told BBC Sport that he would not be automatically against removing the blackout.

"I would still have concerns, because every person through the gate makes a difference," Shotton said.

"I don't think we should just assume it would damage non-league football, but equally you need to know what it could mean for clubs like ours."

Ashington, who have attendances of about 400, see gates rise by up to 25% when Newcastle are not at home - but they already feel the impact of illegal streaming of the Magpies' games.

For the official broadcasters like Sky Sports, these supporters are seen as lost revenue.

There is an argument that the blackout drives piracy. Just how many of those particular fans would pay for a legal subscription is open to debate.

Added to that, there are now many weekends when fewer than 50% of matches in the top two divisions are played at 3pm on a Saturday anyway.

For instance, on 28 November there are just two in the Premier League, and seven in the Championship.

Other non-league clubs, like Dorking Wanders and Hashtag United, have spoken of the opportunities ending the blackout could bring, such as more income streams and fewer inconvenient kick-off times.

But this, for now, seems to be a minority view. The concerns for the health of the entire pyramid, on attendances and finances, are real.

Once the blackout is gone, it is unlikely to come back.

#761. Relive Starship's historic Flight 15 with our best photos from launch and 'Mechazilla' tower catch

We weren't prepared for how stunning some of these turned out.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

STARBASE, Texas — SpaceX has officially wrapped up the 15th test flight of its massive Starship rocket, successfully catching the vehicle's upper stage for the first time.

Flight 15 lifted off from SpaceX's Starbase facility here in South Texas on Friday (Nov. 13). The mission was billed as the first to bring both of Starship's stages, the Super Heavy booster and Ship upper stage, back to the launch site for recovery. And, while SpaceX was forced to divert Super Heavy's return to an off-shore splashdown (and explosion), the upper stage managed to survive its 22-hour jaunt in orbit and plunge through the atmosphere for a picture-perfect catch by the launch tower back at Starbase.

It was the first-ever Ship catch, and a huge milestone toward SpaceX's ultimate goal: making Starship completely reusable.

Liftoff occurred from Pad 2 at 5:47 p.m. EST (2247 GMT; 4:47 p.m. local time) on Friday, against a near cloudless blue sky. Super Heavy is powered by 33 Raptor 3 engines, which provide more than 18 million pounds of thrust at liftoff. And lift off the booster did.

Starship roared off the pad under the power of those Raptors, pulsing visible shockwaves through the plume ejected from the rocket's flame trench.

The first couple minutes of flight went nominally; the vehicle climbed into the sky, gearing up for the hot-staging separation of Super Heavy and Ship — all of which was visible for miles, thanks to the clear Texas skies.

Space.com's images taken from the media’s launch viewing area were shot on a Canon R5 Mark II, with an RF 200-800mm lens that made the sharp pictures of Starship’s liftoff and return possible from almost 4 miles away.

This mirrorless Canon has specs that make it one of the best cameras available right now, with impressive features and functionality, including a 45MP sensor and excellent high-ISO handling.

Check our in-depth Canon R5 Mark II review.

A successful separation occurred at T+2:21 minutes, as Starship soared approximately 40 miles (65 km) overhead. Once disconnected from its booster, Ship increased its thrust and continued onward to space, while Super Heavy, reoriented for its boostback burn and return to Starbase.

That return, however, did not go entirely as planned. Super Heavy experienced a low-fuel alarm and autonomously shifted to an offshore splashdown rather than a catch attempt at Starbase.

Super heavy performed its landing burn above the Gulf of Mexico before cutting its engines for a brief moment and exploding in a giant fireball.

This was an intentional detonation, courtesy of the vehicle's flight termination system.

Ship continued on to low Earth orbit, where it deployed a payload of 26 upgraded Starlink Version 3 satellites. It was the second batch of V3 Starlinks delivered during Starship’s recent flight tests, each of which has added what SpaceX says is the equivalent of 10 Falcon 9 Starlink V2 satellite launches worth of data capacity to its orbital constellation.

Flight 15 was also Starship's second-ever mission to orbit, and its longest so far. Ship spent nearly a full day in orbit, circling Earth a total of 14 times. During its jaunt in space, the spacecraft cleared three separate check points, which allowed SpaceX the opportunity to divert the vehicle for an ocean splashdown if needed, and finally was given the green light to attempt the first-ever Ship tower catch.

At approximately 4:18 p.m. EST (2018 GMT, 3:18 p.m. local time in Texas) on Saturday (Nov. 14), the spacecraft broke through the cloud cover that blanketed the skies above Starbase as onlookers watched its bellyflop plunge toward the ground. Moments after becoming visible, Ship ignited its engines for a flip and burn maneuver, which oriented it upright and swung its trajectory into the tightening grip of the chopstick arms of Starbase's "Mechazilla" launch tower.

After a slight sway back and forth suspended above Earth in Mechazilla's embrace, Ship came to a complete rest, hanging motionless as a historic milestone in SpaceX’s pursuit of fully reusable spaceflight.

It hung there overnight as engineers, and even SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, inspected the spacecraft. Ship was lowered on Sunday (Nov. 15) and transported back to SpaceX's Starbase hanger bay for further checkouts.

SpaceX has not yet said whether Ship 42 will fly again, but its return gives engineers a chance to examine how the spacecraft held up through launch, nearly a day in orbit and atmospheric reentry.

Those findings will help inform upcoming flights as SpaceX ramps up production to continue testing Starship's capabilities.

Josh Dinner is Space.com's Spaceflight Staff Writer and a photographer with a passion for science and exploration. He has worked the space beat since 2016, covering the evolution of NASA's commercial spaceflight partnerships and crewed missions, planetary science missions, the Artemis program and humanity's return to the moon. He also enjoys building 1:144-scale model rockets and spacecraft. Find some of Josh's launch photography on Instagram, and follow him on X, where he mostly posts in haiku.

#759. FA explored legal challenge to Infantino staying on

Gianni Infantino has been leading Fifa since 2016

The Football Association has considered challenging Gianni Infantino's eligibility to run for a fourth term as Fifa president, BBC Sport can reveal.

But it believes any attempt to prevent him from standing in the election in March is likely to fail.

The FA has also confirmed it is backing rival candidate Philippe Diallo.

Infantino oversaw the introduction of a three-term limit when he replaced Sepp Blatter as leader of world football's governing body.

However, Fifa's council agreed in 2022 that his first period in office from 2016 to 2019 should not count as it was the remainder of his predecessor's interrupted final term after resigning.

Earlier this month, human rights campaign group Fair Square wrote to the FA claiming that the decision is open to legal challenge and was "contrary to the spirit and purpose" of Fifa statutes.

It urged the FA to ask Fifa's governance committee to bar Infantino from the election in March because he has already served the maximum three terms.

FA chair Debbie Hewitt has now replied, telling Fair Square that the governing body "has explored the possibility of challenging Mr Infantino's eligibility to run for a further term as the Fifa president but does not consider that such a challenge would secure the outcome sought".

In correspondence seen by the BBC, Hewitt adds: "Ultimately the process followed Fifa's governance and led to an outcome where Mr Infantino's part term was disregarded for the purposes of maximum term limits.

"Having considered the process in detail, we do not believe that a challenge would succeed."

In a statement, Fair Square said: "It's understandable that the FA has no faith in Fifa's internal processes to hold Infantino accountable for serious breaches of the rules, but it's a mistake to abandon these channels, not least because it sends a signal to Infantino that he can do whatever he likes.

"We will encourage the FA to leave its options open where this matter is concerned not least because Debbie Hewitt's position on the Fifa council puts her in a very strong position to demand clear answers on why Fifa discounted Infantino's first term."

Miguel Maduro - a former head of Fifa's governance committee - has said a national association or confederation may need to challenge Infantino's eligibility at the Court of Arbitration for Sport (Cas).

However he has also said that the ability of European football associations to do so has been made harder by Uefa president Aleksander Ceferin deciding to stand for a fourth term earlier this year. Ceferin reversed a previous insistence, in 2024, he would not seek re-election.

The FA was among a number of national associations to withdraw its support of Infantino in the wake of the crisis sparked by his failed plan to sell stakes in the World Cup and other competitions to private investors.

European confederation Uefa has backed rival candidate Diallo, the president of the French Football Federation.

Hewitt, who became a member of Fifa's council in 2023, also told Fair Square that the FA "remains opposed to Mr Infantino's re-election and is committed to providing its full support to Philippe Diallo as our preferred candidate in the upcoming Fifa presidential election".

Last month Hewitt told BBC Sport that Infantino was not fit to lead world football unless he released documents and answered questions relating to the Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) plan.

It has previously referred to the fact that in 2022 its council "unanimously confirmed its agreement with the view of the governance, audit & compliance committee that the period between 2016 and 2019 does not count as a term of office for the current Fifa president, who is therefore about to end his first term".

#758. See Taylor Swift React to CMAs Joke About Travis Kelce Wedding

Taylor Swift burst into laughter when CMA Awards 2026 host Lainey Wilson and longtime pal Brad Paisley made a joke about her and husband Travis Kelce having their wedding at Madison Square Garden.

Taylor Swift was patient zero for wedding jokes at the 2026 CMA Awards.

The 12-time CMA Award winner returned to country music's biggest night for the first time in 10 years on Nov. 18, and couldn't help to laugh when host Lainey Wilson and longtime friend Brad Paisley poked fun at her lavish nuptials with husband Travis Kelce. (Click here to see all the stars at the awards show.)

"I'll never forget what my husband said to me when we went looking for a wedding venue," Wilson, who tied the knot with Devlin "Duck" Hodges in May, shared before breaking out into song with Paisley: "'I beg your pardon, but I never promised you Madison Square Garden.'"

The quip—a play on Lynn Anderson's 1999 hit "I Beg Your Pardon (I Never Promised You A Rose Garden)" and Swift's wedding venue—prompted the "Patient Zero" singer to burst into laughter as she buried her face into pal Brittany Mahomes' shoulder. After regaining her composure, Swift mouthed to Wilson and Paisley, "That was good."

And when Paisley pointed out that he was actually one of the 1,000 guests who attended Swift's wedding, she played along with the bit.

"Remember me?" he asked as the "Blank Space" artist nodded along. "I ate all the shrimp."

But jokes aside, Paisley was touched when he and his wife Kimberly Williams-Paisley received an invite to Swift's wedding, the details of which were shrouded in secrecy in the days leading up to the July 3 ceremony.

"I took this personally when I got the invite, because in the invite, it said, ‘If you’re getting this, you mean a lot to us,’” he told The Associated Press earlier this year. “And it was really fun to watch the cat-and-mouse game of like, ‘We can tell you roughly where it’s gonna be. We’re not gonna say what building.'"

However, according to Paisley, the nuptials ended up being "one of the least-pretentious weddings I’ve ever seen, or ever will see.”

As for why Swift and Kelce picked the 22,000-seater arena for their white veil occasion?

“We wanted to do it somewhere where we could have a very intimate and genuine setting without a lot of distractions,” Kelce explained during a September episode of his New Heights podcast. “We needed it to be a private feel. MSG went above and beyond to give us that.”

"I can’t thank everybody enough that showed up but also that helped put the show on,” Kelce added. “It was so cool to see everyone from my childhood not only mesh with Taylor, but [the people] from her childhood and her family and friends.”

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

On Nov. 16, 1974, humans sent their first message to the stars in an attempt to contact extraterrestrials.

They did this using what was then the largest radio telescope in the world, located at the Arecibo Observatory in Puerto Rico. A group of scientists led by Frank Drake and Carl Sagan sent their message to the M13 star cluster. The message was written in binary code and contained information about human DNA.

It also included figures of a human, the solar system and the Arecibo telescope. The idea was that if any aliens were to receive the signal and figure out how to decode it, they would know where it came from. Because M13 is 25,000 light-years away, it will take 25,000 years for any M13 aliens to hear our message — if they are even out there.

The Arecibo message is only one of several messages intended for extraterrestrials, but this signal sent from Puerto Rico in 1974 was humanity's first intentional olive branch to the stars. At the time, it was the most powerful broadcast ever beamed into space, according to the SETI Institute.

"The broadcast was particularly powerful because it used Arecibo's megawatt transmitter attached to its 305 meter antenna," SETI wrote of the broadcast in a project over. "The emission was equivalent to a 20 trillion watt omnidirectional broadcast, and would be detectable by a SETI experiment just about anywhere in the galaxy, assuming a receiving antenna similar in size to Arecibo's."

The message was designed by astronomy professor Frank Drake of Cornell University (who also developed the famed Drake Equation for alien life), as well as Cornnell graduate students Richard Isaacman and Linda May, and Arecibo staff member James Walker, with input from astronomer Carl Sagan and others, according to Cornell University.

The message included 1,679 bits that were arranged in 73 lines of 23 characters per line, all prime numbers, with the broadcast lasting less than 3 minutes, according to SETI.

As of 2026, the message should have traveled about 52 light-years (1 light-year is the distance light travels in a year), with 24,948 light-years to go before reaching star cluster M13.

The Arecibo message may have been the first message of its kind, but it wasn't the last. We have also included messages on several spacecraft, such as Pioneer and Voyager. NASA and Paul McCartney also beamed a performance of "Across the Universe" in 2008.

#756. Ukrainian FA to blame for failed drugs test - Mudryk

Mudryk joined Chelsea in a deal worth up to Â£89m in January 2023

On-loan Tottenham winger Mykhailo Mudryk says he blames the administration of the Ukraine national team for his failed drugs test and subsequent ban from football.

The 25-year-old, on a season-long loan from Chelsea, was suspended from November 2024 until July 2026 after testing positive for the banned substance meldonium, which he believes entered his system while on international duty.

Having initially faced a four-year ban from the Football Association (FA), his appeal to the Court of Arbitration for Sport was successful.

He returned to football after accepting he had breached anti-doping rules and agreeing to a suspension equivalent to the time he had already served.

After appearing for Chelsea during a pre-season tour of Asia, Mudryk joined Tottenham on transfer deadline day to reunite with his former Shakhtar Donetsk manager Roberto de Zerbi.

In a lengthy interview with the Ukrainian YouTube channel Guest of Gordon, Mudryk was asked who he blamed for his absence from the game.

"The environment, the situation in the Ukrainian national team," he replied. "It should never have existed. I probably haven't said it publicly yet, but I'm saying it now.

"I had never heard of a drug like meldonium. It is a drug you can only get in Eastern Europe. It could only have got into my body in Ukraine. There is no such drug in England."

He explained how he had only been in Ukraine to be with the national team and "it points to the fact it was in a national team camp".

Asked specifically whether he blamed the national team, Mudryk replied: "Yes, exactly."

He also said Ukrainian Association of Football (UAF) president Andriy Shevchenko offered little support, blamed the association for leaks that emerged during the case and claimed its handling of the matter delayed his return to football.

Mudryk also said he spent millions of pounds on legal fees, coaching, pitch hire and private physiotherapy while being unable to access services at Chelsea.

He added: "It was a bolt from the blue. I couldn't believe it [the positive test] was true.

"It was like falling off a skyscraper. In a dream you would hit the ground. In life, I just kept on falling. It hit me very hard, mentally."

Mudryk said he cried and drank alcohol after the initial suspension but never doubted that he would eventually return to top-level football.

BBC Sport has contacted the UAF for comment.

Last year a UAF spokesperson told BBC Sport it was "in close contact with Mudryk's lawyers" but had not been contacted by the FA about the case.

#755. Kings of the jungle? This early human had surprising survival skills that rivalled ours

Homo erectus might have also lived in rainforests — previously thought to be a habitat in which only modern humans could have thrived.Credit: S. Entressangle/E. Daynes/Science Photo Library

Homo erectus is already one of humans’ most extraordinary ancient relatives. The big-brained, tool-wielding species emerged two million years ago in Africa and expanded across Eurasia, before vanishing around 100,000 years ago in Java, Indonesia.

Did Homo erectus and Denisovans mate? Tooth proteins hint at ancient trysts

Did Homo erectus and Denisovans mate? Tooth proteins hint at ancient trysts

Researchers have now added another feather to the hominin’s cap. A pair of studies analysing fossil teeth1,2, which were published in Nature on 18 November, suggest that H. erectus thrived in dense rainforests in southern China as recently as 180,000 years ago.

Researchers had thought that H. erectus was limited to savannahs and open woodlands, says Kira Westaway, a geochronologist at Macquarie University in Sydney, Australia, and a co-author of both studies.

“Never, ever have we seen them in rainforests,” she adds. “This is a really big deal, because we thought Homo sapiens were the only species that had the skill set to survive in really challenging rainforest environments.”

The earliest H. erectus fossils, from eastern Africa, are 1.9 million years old. But the svelte, upright-walking and running hominins wasted little time, reaching western Asia and present-day China some 200,000 years later and modern Java, using land bridges, not long after. The last-known H. erectus remains, from central Java, date to roughly 110,000 years ago3.

Limestone caves in Guangxi province, southern China, contained more than 10,000 fossil teeth.Credit: Kira Westaway (Macquarie University)

While looking for fossils from a three-metre-tall great ape, Gigantopithecus, Westaway and her colleagues identified a pair of limestone caves in Guangxi province, southern China. There, they discovered more than 10,000 fossil teeth from animals such as orangutans (Pongo spp.), monkeys and wild boar (Sus spp.), as well as 9 from hominins. The researchers estimate that the hominins lived between 184,000 and 324,000 years ago, based on dating of both fossils and the surrounding sediments using various methods.

Eight of the hominin teeth resembled those of H. erectus in their shape, a designation that was confirmed by analysing the sequences of proteins preserved in the dental enamel of four specimens, says co-author Frido Welker, a molecular palaeoanthropologist at the University of Copenhagen.

The enamel of the teeth were analysed and their proteins sequenced.Credit: Kira Westaway (Macquarie University)

The ninth lacked the shape and protein signature of H. erectus teeth, says Welker, nor did it resemble those of H. sapiens or Neanderthals (Homo neanderthalensis). Denisovans — the enigmatic ancient humans first discovered in southern Siberia and now linked to diverse fossils from China and elsewhere in Asia — are a possibility, but the evidence is circumstantial, says Welker. “Every label we put on that ninth tooth is a little bit of speculation.”

The multitude of animal teeth was probably accumulated by a scavenger such as a porcupine. The presence of fossils from species such as muntjac deer (Muntiacus muntjac), leopards and orangutans hints at a rainforest environment.

#754. Joint-record six referee errors in last Premier League weekend

The failure to award a penalty to Arsenal would have been more controversial had the Gunners not scored a second-half winner

The Premier League's Key Match Incidents Panel has ruled there were six on-field errors in the last round of games - the joint-highest it has recorded in one weekend.

Each week, the five members of the panel assess all the contentious incidents and vote whether both the referee and the video assistant referee (VAR) have got the decisions correct.

You have to go back to the early part of the 2023-24 season to find the last time there were six mistakes logged.

The statistic does not include correct VAR interventions to fix errors, such as the red card shown to Brentford's Igor Thiago.

In the last round of games almost every fixture had a contentious refereeing situation which was hotly debated.

It started on Friday with a potential penalty to Coventry City for a hair pull by Everton's James Tarkowski.

Arsenal were denied a penalty following a VAR review after it was deemed Kai Havertz was offside.

Tottenham lodged a complaint over a challenge by Leeds United's Jayden Bogle, who was not shown a red card.

And Liverpool argued against a late Crystal Palace penalty.

But which decisions did the KMI Panel rule were incorrect? Some of the votes might surprise you.

Such was the controversy across the weekend, it may come as a surprise that the KMI Panel ruled only two were missed VAR interventions. There have been six missed overall, the same number as this stage last season.

Incident 1: Coventry's Caleb Yirenkyi appeared to have his hair pulled inside the area by Everton's James Tarkowski. No penalty was awarded.

KMI Panel vote: 5:0 incorrect, for the on-field decision and the VAR.

What the KMI Panel said: "Tarkowski had a hold of Yirenkyi's hair and the panel unanimously felt that VAR should have intervened."

Incident 2: Arsenal's Kai Havertz was pulled down inside the area by Hull City's Nobel Mendy. The VAR, Michael Oliver, sent referee Farai Hallam to the pitchside monitor but it was not given due to an offside offence by the Germany international.

KMI Panel vote: 5:0 incorrect, for the on-field decision and the VAR.

What the KMI Panel said: "Although Harvertz is clearly in an offside position, there is a clear and impactful holding action by Mendy before any potential offside offence."

Frank Lampard post-match interview - Everton v Coventry

When the KMI Panel sits down to vote there are two separate considerations.

The first is on the decision of the referee, which is a basic judgement in law and the Premier League's expected interpretation.

The second is on the potential VAR intervention. This takes into account what the referee has said, the available replay angles and the high bar for intervention.

Incident 1: Thierno Barry put Everton in front against Coventry in the 61st minute, but there was a VAR check for a potential handball.

KMI Panel vote: 2:3 incorrect on the field, but 5:0 no VAR intervention.

What the KMI Panel said: "On the balance of probability the ball did accidentally strike Barry's hand. However, the readily available footage did not provide conclusive evidence."

Incident 2: Crystal Palace were awarded a penalty against Liverpool three minutes into stoppage time for a foul by Milos Kerkez on Dario Osorio. But was it just a clash of heads?

KMI Panel vote: 0:5 incorrect on the field, but 5:0 no VAR intervention.

What the KMI Panel said: "A penalty was incorrect with the contact being inevitable. However, it was not a clear and obvious error."

Incident 3: Ipswich were awarded a 72nd-minute penalty against Bournemouth for a foul by Lewis Cook on Abdoul Ouattara.

KMI Panel vote: 1:4 incorrect on the field, but 4:1 no VAR intervention.

What the KMI Panel said: "Ouattara made a clear step across Cook who didn't make a challenge and the referee's decision to award a penalty was incorrect. However, it was not a clear and obvious error."

Incident 4: Potential second yellow card for Bournemouth's Marcus Tavernier.

KMI Panel vote: 2:3 incorrect on the field; no VAR intervention possible.

What the KMI Panel said: "There was a clear, deliberate action by Tavernier to delay the restart."

Some of the most high-profile decisions from across the weekend have not yet featured.

That is because they have been voted to be correct on the field and through VAR.

Incident 1: Leeds United's Jayden Bogle caught Tottenham's Mathys Tel on high on his ankle. There was no VAR review for a red card.

KMI Panel vote: 3:2 correct on the field and for the VAR intervention.

What the KMI Panel said: "The majority felt Bogle was looking to challenge with his right leg and his left leg came down on the back of Tel's ankle without the speed, force or intensity to be serious foul play. Two panellists felt that the challenge was sufficiently dangerous to merit a red card."

Incident 2: Chelsea's Cole Palmer went down on the edge of the area under a challenge by Sunderland's Luke O'Nien.

KMI Panel vote: 4:1 correct on the field and for the VAR intervention.

What the KMI Panel said: "Clear contact made by O'Nien on Palmer which the panel felt should have been penalised with a free-kick on the basis that contact was made outside the area. One panellist felt that the foul contact was inside the area."

Incident 3: Sunderland were awarded a penalty when Levi Colwill was ruled to have tripped Brian Bobbey.

KMI Panel vote: 5:0 correct on the field and for the VAR intervention.

What the KMI Panel said: "There was upper body holding from both players as they progressed into the penalty area before a careless trip by the Chelsea defender."

Incident 4: Possible foul by Senne Lammens on Aston Villa goalkeeper Zion Suzuki before Patrick Dorgu's 96th-minute equaliser.

KMI Panel vote: 5:0 correct on the field and for the VAR intervention.

What the KMI Panel said: "Although Lammens turned away from the ball, the contact he made on Suzuki was not impactful."

The KMI Panel was scrapped this summer in the Scottish Premiership because clubs became frustrated with the voting patterns of its members.

But it is more important in the Premier League, with the results creating a merit table which contributes to 50% of referees' salaries in bonus payments.

Many fans will feel there should have been more than two VAR errors logged in the last round of games.

Yet the KMI Panel does not exist to mirror the opinion of supporters.

Crucially, it uses the laws of the game and how the Premier League expects its games to be refereed as the barometer.

Still, six on-field mistakes - plus the Thiago red card - is clearly a high number.

And fans struggle to understand why it seems to be OK to have these on-field errors, and not correct them due to the high bar.

More than 700 satellites are crossing the sky over an average mid-latitude town at any moment of the night, outnumbering in many cases the stars visible to the naked eye.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

More than 700 satellites are crossing the sky over an average mid-latitude town at any moment of the night, outnumbering in many cases the stars visible to the naked eye.

That's based on an analysis of the trajectories of the 15,833 active satellites that currently circle the planet in low Earth orbit below an altitude of 1,200 miles (2,000 kilometers). Analyzing data from Oct. 12 and 18 this year, researchers found that with a completely unobstructed horizon, 710 satellites were crossing the sky in every single moment of the night above an average U.K. town.

The results were published as a non-peer-reviewed study conducted by engineering firm Accu Components, and is based on satellite monitoring data from the U.S. Space Force available through the public website CelesTrak. Although the researchers specifically focused on the U.K., they say that such heavy satellite traffic flows above most of Europe, the U.S. and other mid-latitude regions, especially between 40 and 50 degrees north or south.

"Most Starlink satellites orbit at around 53 degrees to the equator, so the satellites bunch up over the mid-latitudes. These worldwide figures are approximate, based on a global grid over a single day," Accu Components spokesperson told Space.com in an email. "Skies near the equator are the quietest, with around 490 satellites."

Not all of those satellites are visible to the naked eye, the researchers said in a statement. Because satellites unlike stars don't produce their own light, they must be illuminated by the sun, while the ground below has already sunk into darkness, to be visible. According to the study, an average of 105 satellites out of those 710 were catching light as they zoomed overhead, shining as bright as stars.

The spokesperson said that the actual number of visible satellites varies drastically throughout the night. During the hours after dusk and before dawn, a much greater number of satellites can be seen, while in the middle of the night most no longer catch any light.

"For a typical U.K. town, around 300 satellites are catching the sunlight in the first hour or so after dark," the spokesperson said. "That falls to fewer than 20 around midnight, then climbs back to around 300 before dawn."

For comparison, as little as a few dozen stars are visible to the naked eye in the dead of the night above large, light-polluted megalopolis such as London or New York, according to OwnStarMap. In suburban areas and smaller towns, that number grows to a few hundred. To get to a few thousand visible stars, one must retreat into remote countryside or isolated mountain ranges.

The number of satellites orbiting Earth has grown steeply in the past decade, especially since Elon Musk’s SpaceX began launching its internet-beaming Starlink constellation. Satellite companies plan to launch hundreds of thousands, possibly millions of satellites in the coming decades. If those visions come to pass, the number of passing satellites will vastly outgrow that of stars almost anywhere in the world. The trend especially concerns astronomers who fear the impacts on humankind’s ability to study the Universe.

Satellites crossing the view of ground-based telescopes leave streaks in astronomical images and increase the overall brightness of the sky through the light they reflect down towards Earth. Gradually, even the most powerful telescopes could lose their ability to see the distant stars and galaxies that hold the answers to key questions about the history of the universe.

The study found that throughout the night, an average U.K. town sees 12,891 different satellites passing overhead.

Tereza is a London-based science and technology journalist, aspiring fiction writer and amateur gymnast. She worked as a reporter at the Engineering and Technology magazine, freelanced for a range of publications including Live Science, Space.com, Professional Engineering, Via Satellite and Space News and served as a maternity cover science editor at the European Space Agency.

#752. Alec Baldwin & Hilaria Baldwin Joke Gaslighting Is the Key to Marriage

Alec Baldwin, 68, and Hilaria Baldwin, 42—parents to seven kids together—joked that gaslighting and a good sense of humor are the secret behind their marriage's success.

After 14 years of marriage, Hilaria Baldwin is still Alec Baldwin's rock.

That's why the 30 Rock star and the yoga instructor don't mind teasing each other over the small stuff as they raise their seven kids, Carmen, 13, Rafael, 11, Leonardo, 10, Romeo, 8, Eduardo, 6, María, 5 and Ilaria, 4. In fact, the Baldwins shared why some playful ribbing is the secret to their relationship.

"Gaslighting, but banter," Hilaria told Us Weekly in an interview published Nov. 18. "And then we’re both not sure what’s real and not real anymore, but we both do it to each other."

One harmless example of how they flip the script at home? Hilaria often tries to convince her husband that her frequent redecorating was his idea.

"Every day when he leaves, if I don’t have to work, I come home [and decorate]," she recounted. "I tell him it was his idea, and he’s like, 'Wait a minute.'"

After admitting she eventually persuades the Beetlejuice actor not to worry about the rearranged furniture, she joked, "See, we can both gaslight each other."

And it's that sense of humor that has kept their relationship going strong after the couple's meet-cute in 2011 at a New York City restaurant.

The 42-year-old added of their banter, "It keeps us both getting old very fast and young, both the things at the same time." And Alec, also dad to Ireland Baldwin, 31, with ex Kim Basinger, agreed that their playful rapport is a highlight of the relationship.

"A lot of gaslighting," he teased about rolling with Hilaria's quirks, and vice versa. "The key to a happy marriage is a lot of gaslighting."

And given their sweet bond, it's no surprise Alec's eldest is a big fan of her stepmom.

"She is eccentric and totally bat s--t crazy (in a fun way) but she saved my dad’s life," Ireland wrote in a 2025 post. "She turned his health around and has shown him the forgiveness and kindness that he needed."

And while fans of the Campus Caller actress questioned how having seven younger siblings would impact her relationship with her dad, Ireland gushed about her large family unit.

As she put it, Hilaria "is the reason I get to have siblings/a big family that I’ve always wanted."

Read on for a look inside life with the Baldwins.

Alec Baldwin told the New York Times he gave his future wife, then Hilaria Thomas, his number upon meeting her at Pure Food and Wine in New York in February 2011. The two played phone tag until they finally arranged a time to meet for dinner.

That August they enjoyed their first US Open together, one of Alec's favorite events.

Alec looked into his future and saw Hilaria at the 10th Annual Elton John AIDS Foundation's "An Enduring Vision" benefit at Cipriani Wall Street in October 2011. They moved in together the following month.

Hilaria accompanied Alec to the Cannes Film Festival in 2012. "I've dated a lot of people since my divorce, and have thought a lot about what I wanted and what I wanted to do," he said. "I thought about it too much, I suppose. I wasn't really ready to take that chance and to act until I met Hilaria."

In April 2012, Alec's rep confirmed to E! News that he and Hilaria were engaged.

Hilaria and Ireland Baldwin frequently tweet about their friendship. Ireland joked on the social networking site she was going to serve as a "flower girl" in the wedding, but actually was a bridesmaid.

On June 30, 2012, the happy couple tied the knot in front of family and friends at the Basilica of St. Patrick's Old Cathedral in Manhattan. The bride wore a silk magnolia trumpet Amsale gown and the groom donned a tux from Tom Ford.

The couple are now parents of seven, welcoming Carmen Gabriela (Aug. 23, 2013), Rafael Thomas (June 17, 2015), Leonardo Ángel Charles (Sept. 12, 2016), Romeo Alejandro David (May 17, 2018), Eduardo "Edu" Pao Lucas (Sept. 8, 2020), María Lucía Victoria (Feb. 25, 2021, via surrogate) and Ilaria Catalina Irena (Sept. 22, 2022).

The whole family will be starring on TLC's The Baldwins, premiering Feb. 23, 2025.

#751. Victims of Nazi war in Poland call on Germany for support

More than 80 years after the end of World War II, Polish victims of the Nazi regime are still waiting for a "humanitarian gesture" from Germany. The 2027 draft budget hasn't left them much hope for possible reparations.

"We can no longer wait," declared Polish victims' organizations in a dramatic appeal to German civil society, published on November 5 on the website of the Foundation for Polish–German Reconciliation.

"Around 50,000 survivors of Nazi persecution during the German occupation still live in Poland today. They include former concentration camp and prison inmates, people deported to Germany for forced labor and those subjected to other forms of Nazi repression," wrote the signatories of the appeal.

The open letter pointed out that many of the survivors are over 90 years old, struggling with illness and rising costs, and in need of help in their daily lives. "For many, any further delay in deciding to provide assistance means that help will come too late," said the appeal, which was distributed in German, Polish and English.

While Germany has recognized its moral responsibility toward the remaining survivors of Nazi persecution, the signatories pointed out that a corresponding decision on possible reparations by the German federal government has yet to be made.

"Today, we appeal primarily to German civil society to provide humanitarian support to survivors of Nazi persecution living in Poland," they wrote, addressing businesses, foundations, associations and private citizens. "Every donation matters."

The unresolved issue of war reparations has clouded German-Polish relations for decades.

Following the 1989 democratic transition in Central and Eastern Europe and the reunification of Germany, the federal government provided 500 million deutschmarks to Holocaust victims in Poland. More than 1 million people received support through these funds. Former forced laborers also received payments from the EVZ Foundation, which works to preserve the memory of the victims of National Socialist persecution.

However, given the scale of German crimes during World War II, the reparations provided to date have been considered as insufficient by large parts of Polish society. German occupation policy in Poland was characterized by systematic crimes against the Polish population. An estimated 6 million Polish citizens were killed during the war, including about 3 million Polish Jews.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

As part of the "General Plan East," a large portion of the population was to be displaced, enslaved or murdered. As early as 1939, the "Intelligenzaktion" specifically targeted the Polish elites, including teachers, clergy, civil servants and intellectuals. In addition, approximately 2.5 million Poles were deported to the German Reich for forced labor and made to work there under inhumane conditions.

When it came to power in 2015, Poland's right-wing conservative Law and Justice Party (PiS)  made the issue of war reparations a central focus of Warsaw's policy toward Berlin. The PiS government estimated Poland's war losses at 6.2 trillion zloty (approx. €1.3 trillion/$1.58 trillion) and officially demanded this sum from Berlin in October 2022.

The center-left government led by Donald Tusk has distanced itself from these demands since Tusk's election victory in December 2023. However, the government has also made no secret of the fact that Poland is expecting a "creative solution" from its German partner, according to Foreign Minister Radek Sikorski.

Former German Chancellor Olaf Scholz had offered €200 million ($224 million) prior to his visit to Poland in the summer of 2024, an offer rejected by Tusk as insufficient. The talks held since then between Berlin and Warsaw have failed to produce a solution.

In a final declaration following the German-Polish government consultations in December 2025, the German government promised to "analyze possibilities for additional support for Polish victims of Nazi aggression and the German occupation of Poland."

"Currently, there is no decision regarding a humanitarian gesture and the draft budget reflects this status," Josef Hinterseher, deputy spokesperson for Germany's Federal Foreign Office, told reporters on September 23.

Germany's opposition Greens party has not given up hope of a turnaround in its efforts to secure a "humanitarian gesture."

"Our parliamentary group submitted a request to the budget committee to secure funding for this 'humanitarian gesture.' Unfortunately, the request was rejected," Franziska Brantner, co-chair of the Greens, told DW on Thursday in Warsaw.

"Hope dies last, so we will do everything in our power to ensure that the coalition makes this change after all," she emphasized. Brantner sees the budget committee's "final review session," which will take place this week, as a last chance.

The issue of reparations still plays an important role in Polish society, even more than 80 years after the end of the war. There is hardly a family that did not suffer during the war. In the latest German-Polish Barometer — a representative survey that has been conducted for 25 years — 53% of respondents stated that the suffering of the Polish people is not sufficiently acknowledged in Germany. Only 18% believed that the Germans have done enough.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Jakub Deka, chairman of the Foundation for Polish–German Reconciliation, believes the appeal by the victims' associations could now mobilize Germany's civil society. Following an initial appeal in May directed at the German federal government, several hundred Germans responded with donations ranging from €50 to several hundred euros.

To date, a total of more than €35,000 ($39,000) has been deposited into the foundation's account. Several people in need have already received one-time assistance from this fund. "It's a drop in the bucket, but every little bit helps," Deka told DW.

The foundation's chairman quotes Jerzy Tarasiewicz — who led the victims' association in the Polish city of Gdansk for many years — as a cautionary reminder. In January, Tarasiewicz was quoted in an interview with the daily newspaper Gazeta Wyborcza as saying: "They [the Germans] are waiting for us to die."

Tarasiewicz, who was born in 1942 on a German farm where his parents were performing forced labor, died in late September at the age of 84 without being able to witness this "humanitarian gesture."

"It is a painful reminder that the victims cannot wait any longer," said Deka.

This article was originally written in German.

#750. Taylor Swift Has Surprise Guest for First CMAs Performance in 13 Years

Taylor Swift performed her newest country hit “I Knew It, I Knew You” and one of her oldest “Our Song" at the CMA Awards 2026 in Nashville Nov. 18, marking her first time at the ceremony since 2016.

The CMAs knew Taylor Swift, they knew her.

And now, they have gotten to know her again as the singer took the stage to perform at the Country Music Association Awards Nov. 18 in her first CMAs performance since 2013.

Trading in the yellow Oscar de la Renta gown she wore on the red carpet for a short, white-and-orange frock and cowgirl boots, Swift channeled Toy Story’s cowgirl character Jessie while singing her Toy Story 5 song "I Knew It, I Knew You."

And she went full yee-haw for her country music return, even turning the performance into a mash-up with her 2007 track “Our Song” from her debut album.

Plus, Swift brought a surprise guest, as she was joined on the banjo by Keith Urban, who she previously collaborated on for her 2021 song "That's When (Taylor's Version) (From The Vault)."

“I Knew It, I Knew You" was nominated in the Single of the Year category at this year's ceremony, but ultimately lost out to Ella Langley's "Choosin' Texas." (Click here to for a complete list of winners.)

Swift first revealed she’d be stepping back into her cowboy boots in September, when the Toy Story single received its nomination.

“Looks like I haven’t yee’d my last haw,” she joked in an Instagram Story at the time. “Thank you CMA. See you there.”

Meanwhile, Swift—who last attended the ceremony to bestow Garth Brooks with the Entertainer of the Year honor in 2016—has been living by the message sent in her latest country single, admitting she’s found herself returning to her original genre.

“I love my country roots more and more,” Swift said during a conversation at the Grammy Museum in August. “The further along this path I get and I want to honor them more and more, and I feel more tied and more loyal to them. The people that shaped who I am as an artist and as a writer, that all happened in Nashville.”

And while Swift’s time as a country artist was a slamming screen door for many years following the release of 1989 in 2014, she remembered—no, she never forgot—that she loves country music earlier this year.

“Writing this song felt like a musical departure and coming home at the same time,” Swift mused in a June Instagram post about writing her new country single. “Creating something for Jessie was a new challenge and also felt like second nature all at once.”

For the Grammy winner, it was not only an homage to one of her favorite movie franchises and a return to form, but also a nostalgic joyride.

“We wrote this with so much adoration for these characters that made us laugh,” Swift added, “and helped us learn lessons and think outside the backyard all throughout our childhoods.”

As she has said before, she’ll never change—but she’ll never stay the same, either.

#749. The tightest survival scrap for years? Why it's not too early to worry

Is it too early for the Premier League bottom three to worry?

Despite being only 10 games into the season, sitting in the relegation zone even at this early stage is more worrying than you might think.

But with how tight the Premier League table is, this could also be one of the fiercest relegation battles we have seen in a long time.

Two of the current bottom three, Crystal Palace and Manchester United, will resume their campaigns at the weekend with new managers after appointing Thomas Frank and Mauricio Pochettino respectively.

Sunderland, wedged between the pair in 19th, have not pressed the panic button and have kept faith with Regis le Bris.

But is it too early to worry? We look at what the stats tell us about relegation battles in the past and what we can learn for the months ahead.

Looking at every Premier League season since it changed to a 20-team league in 1995-96, the current bottom three have cause to be concerned.

In 19 of the previous 31 seasons (61%), only one of the bottom three sides after 10 games managed to avoid relegation.

For fairness and accuracy, the 'bottom three' are the three sides with the worst record after 10 games, not simply those in the relegation zone after matchweek 10, since in some seasons a team had played nine games by that point.

Only in 10 seasons (32%) have two or more of the bottom three stayed up - and that has not happened in any of the past eight campaigns. The last time more than one team avoided the drop was in 2017-18, when all three survived.

That has only happened twice, although only twice have all three sides been relegated.

Overall, of the 93 previous teams in the bottom three after 10 games, 41 survived and 52 were relegated - a survival rate of 44%.

This is the third time that Palace have been bottom after 10 games. On both previous occasions, they did not just survive but thrived, finishing 11th.

They did so under Tony Pulis in 2013-14 and under Roy Hodgson in 2017-18. Both managers, like Frank, were appointed early in the season following poor starts under Ian Holloway and Frank de Boer respectively.

The 2013-14 season is the only previous time that Sunderland and Palace were the bottom two at this stage. The Black Cats also survived thanks to a great, late escape under Gus Poyet.

This is the first time United have been in the bottom three after 10 games of a Premier League season.

Given the size and resources of the club, it is unlikely they will go down, although the team in 18th place at this stage have been relegated in each of the past six seasons.

Fans of all three clubs will hope for a repeat of 2017-18, when not only Palace but the bottom three improved significantly to finish comfortably mid-table.

While history suggests only one of the bottom three will survive, there is also evidence to suggest that this might not be a standard Premier League season.

Palace have seven points, which is the most the bottom side after 10 games have had for 24 years. The bottom three all had eight points in 2002-03.

Sunderland's eight points is also the most that a side in 19th place have had for 16 years. Wolves had nine points in 2010-11 and survived in 17th.

In fact, only five points separate the bottom half of the Premier League, with Tottenham in 11th on 12 points and Palace bottom with seven â the smallest gap at this stage for 24 years.

The highest that a team in the bottom three after 10 games have finished the season is eighth - Bolton in 2003-04, Tottenham in 2008-09 and Everton in 2017-18 - which suggests it will be Conference League at best for Manchester United next season.

Then again, the table is so tight that only nine points separate Chelsea in fifth and Palace - the smallest gap at this stage for 16 years.

Given that fifth place has been enough to qualify for the Champions League in recent seasons, optimistic United fans may not be ruling it out just yet.

That means even sides who have started well could be involved in the relegation battle.

The most points a team have had after 10 games of a 38-game season and been relegated is 14 - Joe Royle's Manchester City in 2000-01.

The most recent team to start well but be relegated were Eddie Howe's Bournemouth in 2019-20, who were sitting pretty in ninth with 13 points at this stage but went down on the final day.

As mentioned, this season has both the 'best' bottom side in terms of points and the most compact bottom half of the table that we have seen at this stage since 2002-03.

In that season, West Ham were relegated on the final day with 42 points - the most a side have been relegated with in Premier League history.

Given the way this season is shaping up, 40 points might also not be enough to survive.

Reflect Orbital is moving forward with its plan to place mirrors in Earth orbit to produce and sell sunlight after dark.

The goal is to extend the hours and output of solar farms globally, "making clean power dispatchable and available when you need it," the California-based startup explains on its website.

Reflect Orbital has made significant progress to date. On Tuesday (Nov. 10), for example, the company announced it had secured $73.5 million in new funding, boosting its total raise to more than $100 million. It has also gotten a formal go-ahead from the U.S. government to try out the concept in space and is currently readying its first test satellite, which is expected to launch in the second quarter of 2027. The identity of the launch provider is being kept under wraps at this time, the firm told Space.com.

Reflect Orbital recently conducted a ground-based test in California, lighting up a mountainous area to practice search and rescue (SAR) techniques.

On Oct. 10, the space startup set up spotlights near Lone Pine, California to simulate the illumination its proposed satellites could provide — controlled lighting without the need for any ground infrastructure. "This lighting will support a variety of customers, from remote search-and-rescue operations to solar farms generating clean power," the company explained in an Oct. 14 statement.

The October illumination test ran from 7 p.m. to midnight and involved members of the China Lake Mountain Rescue Group (CLMRG), who practiced with night-time equipment.

CLMRG is an all-volunteer activity, operating under the auspices of the Kern County Sheriff's Office providing SAR services on an on-call basis at no cost.

"Together with local search-and-rescue and disaster response groups, we carried out a fully permitted nighttime demonstration of our responsive lighting service," a Reflect Orbital spokesperson told Space.com in response to an inquiry about the exercise. "Search-and-rescue and disaster response teams are expected to be our first customers, so this was a real-world test conducted alongside teams who will use our technology."

Mobile lighting gear was mounted on Horseshoe Meadows Road to provide a spot of light similar to the ones that Reflect Orbital satellites are expected to deliver. "The aim was to create a precise, realistic simulation of our service, so emergency responders could see how it will perform in real scenarios," Reflect Orbital said.

The brightness of the spot was roughly 0.7 lumens.

Reflect Orbital added that it will keep working closely with local communities and authorities wherever the company operates, to show how its technology can help save lives.

"We're committed to learning incrementally about our technology and its impacts, and from potential customers and stakeholders, ahead of our planned satellite operations," the company stated.

In last month's illumination experiment, Reflect Orbital secured permits in advance, filed a NOTAM (a notice to pilots), notified Edwards Air Force Base and coordinated with the local sheriff's department. Area residents were also notified about the test ahead of time.

In a related development, Reflect Orbital has announced the purchase of two Skyroot Aerospace launches to deploy some of its spacecraft. Skyroot's Vikram-1 launcher is a product of India's private space sector, first flying from the nation's Sriharikota launch site last July. That flight was a landmark success, as Vikram-1 became the first private Indian rocket ever to reach orbit.

"These dedicated launches provide assured schedule and capacity, and complement Reflect Orbital's other planned launches from sites in the United States," Reflect Orbital explained in a different Oct. 14 statement.

Reflect Orbital says its approach is "incremental and test-and-learn." The company has been granted a license from the U.S. Federal Communications Commission (FCC) for one satellite. That mission will test the technology, including built-in safeguards governing precisely how, where and when the sunlight service is delivered.

"It will provide real-world data that shapes the design of future satellites," Reflect Orbital said, "the markets we serve, how we engage communities and the operational practices we put in place. We expect this to be the first of several test missions."

Reflect Orbital wants to be operating at least 50,000 of its mirror satellites in orbit by 2035. Not surprisingly, many people in the astronomy and stargazer communities have a dim view of this plan, saying it will generate light pollution that significantly degrades the night sky.

Reflect Orbital counters that most people and most places will never see this light. Customers will require permits, signoff from local authorities and "Know Your Customer compliance" to receive the service. Every service will require multi-layer approval, the company says, and if people do not want the light, they will not receive it.

Reflect Orbital also claims that it can maintain exclusion zones covering astronomical observation sites.

"Our satellites will be default-off when idle and constellation vehicles are designed to stay under +7 stellar magnitude for all non-serving attitudes. We're able to dim the brightness of the service and turn it off at any stage," the company's website states.

Reflect Orbital also notes that it's an industry member of the International Astronomical Union's (IAU) Center for the Protection of the Dark and Quiet Sky.

The company says that it's collaborating with the IAU on an observing campaign for when the service is operational and is also working on a coordination agreement with the U.S. National Science Foundation.

"We've engaged extensively with scientists, astronomers, environmental researchers and other stakeholders," Reflect Orbital stated. "Their feedback has meaningfully informed the design of our spacecraft and operational plans. We continue to welcome scientific exploration of how novel technology could deliver a lot of benefits to the world."

Leonard David is an award-winning space journalist who has been reporting on space activities for more than 50 years. Currently writing as Space.com's Space Insider Columnist among his other projects, Leonard has authored numerous books on space exploration, Mars missions and more, with his latest being "Moon Rush: The New Space Race" published in 2019 by National Geographic. He also wrote "Mars: Our Future on the Red Planet" released in 2016 by National Geographic. Leonard  has served as a correspondent for SpaceNews, Scientific American and Aerospace America for the AIAA. He has received many awards, including the first Ordway Award for Sustained Excellence in Spaceflight History in 2015 at the AAS Wernher von Braun Memorial Symposium. You can find out Leonard's latest project at his website and on Twitter.

Tim McGraw had two special guests with him on the red carpet at the Nov. 18 CMA Awards in Nashville: daughters Maggie, 28, and Audrey, 24. The trio were also joined by mom Faith Hill inside the show.

Tim McGraw was happy to just see his daughters smile at the 2026 CMA Awards.

The “I Like It, I Love It” singer was joined by his and wife Faith Hill’s daughters Maggie, 28, and Audrey, 24, for the Nov. 18 ceremony as the trio walked the red carpet together before being joined by Faith inside the Bridgestone Arena in Nashville.
