When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

We're in a bit of a cyberpunk revival at the moment. 2026 gave the excellent second season of Netflix’s "Cyberpunk: Edgerunners," and Prime Video's "Blade Runner 2099" is just around the corner. 2027 will continue this trend with "Neuromancer" blasting onto Apple TV.

Based on cyberspace guru William Gibson’s seminal 1984 novel, "Neuromancer" follows Case, a brilliant hacker who falls into a web of digital espionage and crime as he attempts an impossible corporate heist. The pulp noir novel has been hailed as a generational revelation, and its slang and terminology have become ingrained in computer nerd subcultures.

After decades of development hell and failed attempts at various studios, "Neuromancer" and its plugged-in digital dystopia are finally jacking into the small screen in January 2027.

Apple TV is already the secret home of amazing sci-fi, and "Neuromancer" will join the streamer's impressive roster of science fiction stalwarts like "Foundation", "Silo", "Invasion", "Dark Matter", "Murderbot", "For All Mankind", "Pluribus", and "Star City."

Can it live up to the hype? We won't have to wait long for an answer. In the meantime, let's jack into cyberspace and scour the code for everything we know about Apple TV's "Neuromancer!"

Apple TV+’s Neuromancer officially powers up on Jan 22, 2027.

It was first announced to be in full production back on July 1, 2025, which actually coincided with the 41st anniversary of the publication of William Gibson's absorbing book.

Filming took place in Tokyo, Los Angeles, Istanbul, Canada, and London to create a truly international flair to replicate the novel’s action.

Travelling outside the US and still want access to Neuromancer? Good news: NordVPN can help you get around those pesky geo-blocking restrictions so you can watch the streaming service you've paid for anywhere in the world.

Gibson's "Neuromancer" is a dense, jargon-heavy juggernaut of a book that demands intense concentration to absorb all the slang, lingo, computer terms, and staccato literary rhythms, but it's a fantastic immersion into a fully fleshed-out world. It's also worryingly prophetic, showing a world not unlike ours today in 2026.

"Neuromancer's" TV iteration seems to be following the novel closely and will center around Case, a brilliant, cocky, neurologically damaged hacker who is forced into a logistical quagmire of digital corporate espionage with his cyber-enhanced partner Molly after embezzling cash from an employer.

Molly is a "razor-girl" mercenary with mirrored eyes who dreams of attempting a dangerous heist against a nefarious corporate dynasty hiding deep, dark secrets. Hackers (known as console cowboys) "jack in" to guarded computer systems using sophisticated software and surgically implanted ports to bypass firewalls and security protocols.

Molly’s mysterious client is Armitage, a former black ops military operative with a shadowy past. The team’s prime target is a next-generation super AI entity named Wintermute.

Everything goes smoothly until it doesn’t, and Case and Molly are soon running for their lives before eventually coming into contact with Wintermute’s AI sibling, called Neuromancer. A merger of the two systems seems inevitable, and the crux of the narrative is focused on that certainty.

The first cryptic teaser trailer for "Neuromancer" landed back on July 1, 2025, to mark the start of filming.

Revealed in the brief video was a murky cocktail watering hole that springs to life in a flourish of humming lights and tinkling pinball machines. A bright blue-and-orange neon sign blinks on in the back, spelling out the name Bar Chatsubo, the iconic Chiba City hacker lounge that's well known to dedicated readers of the 1984 novel.

A second teaser came on July 6, 2026, in which a retro computer was powered up to display the opening sentence of Gibson’s book, describing the dour atmosphere of Japan's Chiba City... "The sky above the port was the color of television, tuned to a dead channel."

It's such a classic line that perfectly reflects that bleak cyberpunk mood.

Then, on July 25, 2026, Apple TV released the first full teaser (or short trailer) that revealed much of the series' visual style, the mega-city setting, and the main cast of Callum Turner, Brianna Middleton, and Mark Strong.

It’s got a serious edge and attitude that sets the tone with bold graphics and enticing sounds.

"Neuromancer’s" eclectic cast is a mix of fresh faces and wily veterans that includes:

"Neuromancer" was co-created for TV by Graham Roland ("Tom Clancy's Jack Ryan," "Dark Winds") and J.D. Dillard ("Devotion," "The Outsider," "Sleight").

It’s a 10-episode prestige series collaboration between Skydance Television and Anonymous Content that's also produced by Drake's production company, DreamCrew Entertainment. Graham Roland serves as "Neuromancer's" showrunner, with J.D. Dillard inked to direct the pilot episode and perhaps other installments.

"We're incredibly excited to be bringing this iconic property to Apple TV+," executive producers Roland and Dillard announced last year in a statement.

"Since we became friends nearly 10 years ago, we've looked for something to team up on, so this collaboration marks a dream come true. 'Neuromancer' has inspired so much of the science fiction that's come after it, and we’re looking forward to bringing television audiences into Gibson's definitive 'cyberpunk' world.”

#725. Microbiome home tests are taking off. Can they be trusted?

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Amber Dance is a freelance science writer near Los Angeles, California.

A mix of microorganisms from a human faecal sample, imaged using a scanning electron microscope. Credit: Steve Gschmeissner/Science Photo Library

First, the good news: I have 133 microbial species living in my gut. That’s a collection that ranks as ‘excellent’ according to NirvanaBiome, the company in Germantown, Maryland, that analysed my stool sample. The firm based its rating on the overall diversity of my gut’s residents plus my levels of specific beneficial and undesirable species.

Revealed: how this common gut microbe protects against heart disease

Revealed: how this common gut microbe protects against heart disease

But then came a second, less promising assessment: Viome in Bellevue, Washington, identified only 61 kinds of active microorganism in my gut and suggested that some of them were not performing optimally. Viome recommended dietary changes and offered customized supplements to improve my health.

I was intrigued by the results, but also flummoxed by the different messages. That’s not an uncommon response, says microbiologist Rob Knight, director of the Center for Microbiome Innovation at the University of California, San Diego. When scientists tested a handful of microbiome testing kits alongside one another in formal studies, they found wide discrepancies in the results. These differences make it hard to understand or really trust the findings from any given provider, says Diane Hoffmann, director of the Law and Health Care programme at the University of Maryland in Baltimore, who co-authored one of those studies.

The companies stand by their products. “Of course there’s variability,” says Kelly Moffat, chief operations officer for Cmbio in Germantown, which does the laboratory work and genetic sequencing for NirvanaBiome. “There has to be because this is complex testing.”

Momo Vuyisich, chief science officer at Viome’s lab in Bothwell, Washington, also says he was unsurprised by the degree of variation found by formal studies. Labs use different methods to extract, sequence and analyse microbial genetic material. Viome, for example, sequences RNA rather than DNA, allowing it to uncover microbial gene activity, rather than only the presence of genes. Vuyisich argues that this is more relevant to human health. And he says that although every method will have biases, as long as a consumer sticks with the same provider, it should produce results that are comparable over time.

Interest in these kinds of test is booming. “There’s so much public enthusiasm and excitement about the microbiome,” says Knight. Some customers are simply curious about the microscopic beings that live inside them and potentially affect their health; others have health conditions such as irritable bowel syndrome and hope that their gut microbes will reveal the underlying cause or a path to better health.

Although people can order the tests and follow their recommendations without the help of a medical professional, some people are bringing the findings to their physicians. “I groan when I see someone come in with a microbiome test,” says Fergus Shanahan, a gastroenterologist and immunologist at University College Cork in Ireland, who has spent much of his career studying the microbiome. For someone struggling with gut health, a consumer microbiome profile isn’t usually specific enough to help. And if there’s a concern about an infection, such as Clostridioides difficile, it’s more straightforward to test for known pathogens than to assess the entire microbial community.

The tantalizing links between gut microbes and the brain

The tantalizing links between gut microbes and the brain

Microbiologists and gasteroenterologists who spoke to Nature generally agreed that microbiome testing has the potential to both reflect and promote health, but many said that the science isn’t yet mature enough to support microbiome testing for most consumers. In their view, the limited clinical usefulness of today’s consumer tests can make them poor value for money (costing around US$100–300). The specialists warn that acting on advice that doesn’t come from clinicians could lead customers to adopt unnecessarily restrictive diets or delay appropriate medical assessment. Critics say that consumer microbiome testing needs more regulatory scrutiny and oversight.

“This is an industry that’s running wild,” says genomicist Jacques Ravel, director of the Center for Advanced Microbiome Research and Innovation at the University of Maryland School of Medicine in Baltimore and a co-author on one of the studies that tested several providers. With regards to testing methods, he says, “there’s no standard”.

Moffat says, “I think the jury’s out on exactly what it is that we can actionably do today based on this data.” But she says that microbiome profiles, combined with other testing such as gut metabolomics, could yield interesting and useful health information.

The gut microbiome has emerged as an incredible correlate of overall health. From immune-system function to metabolism, skin disorders and mental health, study after study has found links between a person’s well-being and the trillions of microbes that live in their digestive tract. The premise of a head count of these species and assessment of their actions, to monitor and improve gut health in a personalized way, certainly sounds appealing. Viome’s website, for example, promises: “No more trial and error … Follow a plan built precisely for you.”

Companies can identify species and, on the basis of those lists, infer what the microbes are probably doing, such as manufacturing metabolites or inciting inflammation. But running even the simplest microbiome testing is expensive, says Alessandra Cervino, research director at PiLeJe, a science-based food-supplement company in Paris. She says her microbiome testing company, Luxia Scientific, closed in 2024 for financial reasons.

Some microbiome testing firms recommend fermented foods, such as kombucha, for gut health.Credit: Deb Lindsey for The Washington Post via Getty

Many testing companies also offer lifestyle and nutritional advice or sell supplements. For example, Viome analysed diverse functions performed by the microbes in my gut, such as digestive efficiency, gas production and serotonin manufacture. I then received a detailed eating plan — which told me to eschew broccoli and load up on pecans, among other suggestions — along with an offer for precision supplements and probiotics with a price tag of more than $150 a month. Although it’s hard to change the composition of microbes in one’s gut, alterations in diet or even simply ageing can shift their activities, says Vuyisich. The company recommends re-testing every four to six months to check for shifts and update the plan.

He points to 19 peer-reviewed publications by Viome as evidence of the company’s rigour (see go.nature.com/4actdhq). For example, the firm’s analysis for consumers is supported, in part, by published data on how gut microbes influence individuals’ responses to glucose in various foods, based on 550 people in the United States who collectively ate more than 30,000 meals while wearing glucose monitors1. The company validated those findings in a further cohort in Japan, Vuyisich says, but those data are not published.

Microbiome tests are not created equal, says Tim Spector, a physician-scientist at King’s College London and co-founder of London-based ZOE, which offers microbiome testing and a supplement in addition to a gut-health app that I’ve been playing with. ZOE’s products, Spector says, are backed by research on thousands of people. “There definitely are some not-so-good players out there that give this field a bad name,” he says. “It’s not easy to do this well.”

There are also several ways to do microbe testing; companies take varying approaches that yield disparate results, as at least two studies have shown. Scientists at the US National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) in Gaithersburg, Maryland, shipped homogenized stool samples from one person to seven companies2. NIST’s remit is researching and applying standards for measurement. This experiment was a step towards understanding the diversity of testing options out there, says one of the study authors, NIST microbiologist Stephanie Servetas, who is based in Sheridan, Wyoming. The researchers didn’t name the companies in their report because they wanted to focus attention on the comparison between tests rather than perceived accuracy of any individual provider.

The result: “Companies produce strikingly different results,” says co-author Scott Jackson, a molecular geneticist who used to direct the NIST microbiology program and is now a consultant in Saint Michaels, Maryland. “They couldn’t even agree on what’s healthy and unhealthy,” Jackson says. The microbe lists ranged from 34 to 906 identified genera; only 3 of which showed up in all reports. In fact, the results were as varied from company to company as they would be for different people, despite all tests being done on samples from the same individual.

A European and Canadian team obtained similar outcomes when they sent homogenized samples from one person’s stool to six companies, also anonymized. Three companies rated the microbial diversity as “excellent” or “good”; two called it “average”; one said it was “unfavourable”3. The results were so variable, that at least some of them must be lacking in validation or standardization, says co-author Céline Druart, executive director of the Pharmabiotic Research Institute (PRI) in Brussels, a non-profit organization specializing in regulation of microbiome innovations. “It’s very difficult to make a conclusion,” she says.

How gut bacteria could boost cancer treatments

How gut bacteria could boost cancer treatments

This broad divergence in results is not surprising, says Jack Gilbert, director of the Microbiome and Metagenomics Center at the University of California, San Diego. The variation starts at sampling: scoop a bit of faecal matter into a tube, stab it with a coring device or swipe the sampler across some used toilet paper; ship it off as-is, or in some kind of preservative (as both Viome’s and NirvanaBiome’s kits asked me to). Each option could influence the balance of the microbes that are collected and what survives to be sequenced.

In the lab, Servetas says the method by which the researchers extract genetic material from a sample is a big source of divergence. Gentler protocols will bias a sample towards microbes that are easy to crack open, whereas harsher methods will capture a higher share of species with tougher exteriors.

After sequencing, another major source of difference, says Knight, is the bioinformatics pipeline that labs use. What length or number of genetic sequences is required to consider a microbe present? What list of sequences and microbes are they using as a reference? “All bets are off when you then computationally analyse it with your favourite method,” says Knight.

Would companies support having standards to validate their tests? “We are really big advocates on really having a standard here,” says Kimberley Sukhum, chief science officer at Tiny Health in Austin, Texas, which offers gut microbiome tests as well as vaginal microbiome tests.

But it’s hard to set those standards, in part because there is no known ‘ground truth’ for a natural microbial sample. Compare that with, say, a blood-glucose test; a lab can get a known value from a standard sample either right or wrong. But the microbiome, in its glorious complexity, does not allow for such simple validation. NIST has used mixed human donor samples to develop a standard4. And Tiny Health has experimented with generating a reference for benchmarking from synthetic communities. It was built from individual microbial species rather than sampled from faeces5. But neither of those standards is exactly like the microbiome of an individual person.

Even if labs could assess a microbiome perfectly, they’d still have a problem: there’s no defined healthy microbiome like there is one range of healthy blood-glucose levels. Each person’s microbiome is unique, like a fingerprint. There are infinitely many ways to have a healthy microbiome, and infinitely many ways to have an unhealthy one, says Shanahan; it’s not entirely clear how to draw a line between the two.

How gut microbes could drive brain disorders

How gut microbes could drive brain disorders

Companies must compare customer microbiomes with some standard of health, but these vary too. They might be based on past customers or large, public databases. But microbiomes differ considerably depending on factors such as ethnicity, sex, age, recent antibiotic use or even whether someone was born by caesarean section.

#724. Bryan Freedman Sued Over Hush-Money Deals Shielding Michael Jackson Estate

The Cascio siblings claim the attorney had a conflict of interest when he brokered their settlements with the singer's estate.

Five siblings at the forefront of sexual assault allegations against Michael Jackson have sued Bryan Freedman, Hollywood’s favorite lawyer who was allegedly enlisted by the pop star’s estate to deceive them into signing hush-money deals.

In a lawsuit filed on Wednesday in California state court, Frank Cascio and his siblings Edward, Dominic, Aldo and Marie-Nicole accuse Freedman of legal malpractice, breach of fiduciary duty and fraud. They allege that he duped them into signing agreements barring them from publicly discussing Jackson’s alleged abuse that have emerged as obstacles in ongoing litigation against the estate, which Freedman allegedly worked for while representing the siblings when the deals were signed in 2019.

The siblings’ relationship with Freedman started five years earlier when a lawsuit was filed against Edward, who at the time was defending the singer from sexual abuse allegations, and the estate in connection to his work on a posthumous Jackson album. At the recommendation of the estate, which paid for legal fees, he retained Freedman, according to the complaint.

The lawsuit says Jackson’s estate again turned to Freedman to broker deals with the Cascio siblings in the wake of Leaving Neverland, which featured sexual abuse allegations against the singer. Freedman told the siblings that they didn’t need to hire their own lawyer and that the settlement was fair and nonnegotiable, according to the complaint.

“None of this was true,” writes Howard King, a lawyer for the siblings, in the filing. “At the time, Freedman represented the estate, including in connection with litigation against HBO, which had broadcast Leaving Neverland.”

The document the estate presented framed the settlement as an “acquisition and consulting agreement,” identifying the deal as a purchase of the family’s life story rights, the lawsuit says. Under the terms of the contract, the estate made five annual payments of $690,000 to each sibling. In exchange, they are barred from publicly discussing Jackson’s alleged sexual abuse and subject to mandatory arbitration provisions, among other things that include releasing the estate and its representatives from potential liability. It requires the entire family to return all payments if one member is violates the terms of the deal, according to the complaint.

The siblings say they learned of Freedman’s alleged conflict of interest when the lawyer in 2024 told them that the estate hadn’t paid enough money five years earlier. He allegedly called the deal “toilet paper” and that he “had enough on the estate” that would convince its representatives to “do right” by them, the lawsuit says. After Freedman instructed the siblings to hire him, they retained another lawyer, who told the estate that the 2019 deals would be challenged. The estate later filed an arbitration demand against the siblings for breaching the nondisparagement and confidentiality provisions of their deal.

“If Freedman had not fraudulently induced Plaintiffs into signing the agreement, they never would have been dragged into litigation for publicly discussing Jackson’s abuse,” states the complaint, which notes that a child sex trafficking lawsuit they had filed against the estate was forced into arbitration under the terms of the 2019 agreement.

The lawsuit was filed as Freedman, who didn’t respond to a request for comment, fields accusations of helping orchestrate online smear campaigns in public relations battles against his clients’ adversaries. A trial is scheduled to start next year involving Rebel Wilson and producer Amanda Ghost, who accuses the actress and her public relations team of creating a site that accused Ghost of sex trafficking.

#723. The Biggest Snubs & Surprises at the 2026 CMA Awards

The pundits didn't guess every category correctly.

Everyone expected Ella Langley to sweep the 2026 CMA Awards, and sure enough, she did, setting a new, all-time record of six awards in one night. That broke the old record of five awards in one night first set by Johnny Cash in 1969 and then tied by Vince Gill in 1993, Alan Jackson in 2002 and Lainey Wilson in 2023.

But that doesn’t mean there were no snubs or surprises at the awards show, which was held at Bridgestone Arena in Nashville on Wednesday (Nov. 18) and hosted by Wilson for the third year in a row (second year in a row as solo host).

The show opened with a tribute to Dolly Parton, who died in August, with Vince Gill and Wilson singing the country icon’s 1974 classic “I Will Always Love You.” There was also a tribute to John Anderson, who died in October, with Dierks Bentley and Zach Top singing his 1983 hit “Swingin.’”

Perhaps because it was the show’s 60th anniversary, there were several backward-looking performances. Taylor Swift included a bit of her 2007 hit “Our Song” (her first No. 1 hit on Billboard’s Hot Country Songs chart) in her performance of her current hit “I Knew It, I Knew You.” Tim McGraw performed his 1994 hit “Don’t Take the Girl” (his first No. 1 on Hot Country Songs). Tucker Wetmore performed Hank Williams Jr.’s 1984 hit “All My Rowdy Friends Are Coming Over Tonight.” Brooks & Dunn performed a hit medley.

But let’s get back to what you came for: Here are snubs and surprises from the 2026 CMA Awards.

Musgraves went 0-5 on the night. She had more nominations without a win than anyone else this year. Musgraves hasn’t won a CMA Award since 2019. But she and Lambert teamed for a winning performance on their song “Horses and Divorces,” about two people who managed to mend a fractured friendship.

Most pundits figured Tucker Wetmore would win best new artist of the year. Wetmore had won new male artist of the year at the ACM Awards six months ago. But in a major surprise the award went to Stephen Wilson Jr. (who, at 47, set a new record as the oldest winner in the history of the category).

Both Wilson and Wetmore were nominated for new artist of the year last year as well, losing to Zach Top. (The CMA gives artists two shots at the award in this category.)

We all knew voters would be “Choosin’ Texas” every chance they could, but Ella Langley’s album of the year win for Dandelion was less assured. She beat two past winners in that category – Kacey Musgraves, who was nominated for Middle of Nowhere, and Luke Combs, nominated for The Way I Am. Musgraves won in 2018 for Golden Hour; Combs won twice, in 2020 for What You See Is What You Get and in 2022 for Growin’ Up.

The other nominees in the stacked category were Zach Top’s Ain’t in It for My Health and an eponymous album by Parker McCollum.

You couldn’t call it a big surprise when Chris Stapleton won male vocalist of the year. After all, he had won in the category eight times previously. But Stapleton didn’t win the award last year, and Billboard’s country experts Melinda Newman and Jessica Nicholson called it for Zach Top and Cody Johnson, respectively.

But Stapleton took the award, becoming the first winner in the history of the category to have three separate stints as a winner. He won every year from 2015-18, then lost to Luke Combs in 2019 and 2020, before winning again from 2021-24. He lost to Johnson last year but came back to win again this year.

"Our tests have shown that a device weighing just 50 grams can deliver millimeter-level ranging precision."

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A British startup thinks it can help humanity deal with its space junk problem.

Millions of pieces of space debris circle Earth at the moment, according to the European Space Agency (ESA). Even the smallest fragments are potentially dangerous, given how fast stuff travels in orbit.

Experts have proposed a range of measures to deal with this junk. The smallest bits, for example, may require big space nets, or lasering the stuff down to Earth. Large satellites are increasingly being deliberately deorbited these days, and a few have even been refueled to keep them operating in orbit — something that will likely start happening more and more over the coming years.

Now, the British startup Foundational has another idea to throw into the mix: retroreflectors. The company argues that its tech can help fight the space-junk problem — and it just proved out a demo version in an orbital test.

London-based Foundational recently tested its Retro-2 laser retroreflector system, which it developed in collaboration with ESA. The early-stage test was designed to ensure that Foundational's retroreflectors can return laser-ranging signals from a satellite, at altitudes between about 600 kilometers and 870 kilometers (about 370 to 540 miles), with a usable range distance of 300 to 1,400 km (186 to 870 miles).

The long-term aim is to create a sort of tracking device for spacecraft, so they can be monitored in orbit even after they fall silent.

The tech, Foundational said in a statement today (Nov. 17), needs "no electronics, power or commands from its host spacecraft" and allows ground stations to keep tabs on the orbiting spacecraft.

The demo mission launched this past July on SpaceX's Transporter-17 rideshare flight. It attached Retro-2 — a mini device with seven reflectors — to a small satellite that was integrated into an ION carrier craft operated by the Italian company D-Orbit.

Retro-2 worked as advertised, successfully returning 6,111 laser shots beamed from the from the ground across five passes in low Earth orbit.

"Our tests have shown that a device weighing just 50 grams [1.8 ounces] can deliver millimeter-level ranging precision," Dave Gooding, Foundational's co-founder and chief technical officer, said in today's statement. "As space becomes increasingly crowded, keeping satellites trackable throughout their lifetime and beyond is critical to managing collision risks."

Foundational is in its early stages — it was founded in 2025 and just emerged from stealth last month. Nevertheless the company has already raised £8.2 million ($10.9 million) in pre-seed funding.

Foundational is part of a range of companies involved in debris removal, satellite servicing or debris tracking that have raised funds in 2026. Others include Starfish Space (which raised more than $100 million in a Series B), Katalyst Space ($12 million in funding) and international companies like India's Cosmoserve Space.

Elizabeth Howell (she/her), Ph.D., was a staff writer in the spaceflight channel between 2022 and 2024 specializing in Canadian space news. She was contributing writer for Space.com for 10 years from 2012 to 2024. Elizabeth's reporting includes multiple exclusives with the White House, leading world coverage about a lost-and-found space tomato on the International Space Station, witnessing five human spaceflight launches on two continents, flying parabolic, working inside a spacesuit, and participating in a simulated Mars mission. Her latest book, "Why Am I Taller?" (ECW Press, 2022) is co-written with astronaut Dave Williams.

#721. Germany slips in climate protection rankings as other countries make gains

Record renewable energy growth is driving climate progress in some countries, but Germany and many major emitters are falling behind.

Germany has slipped down the climate action ranking for the third consecutive year, with the former green leader now being outperformed by Brazil, Colombia and Romania.

In its worst performance since 2019, the country fell to place 25 and received a "medium" rating overall on the yearly Climate Change Performance Index (CCPI), which assesses efforts to curb global warming in 64 countries plus the European Union.

Still, "a number of countries have been making good progress for years," said Jan Burck, CCPI lead author, in a statement. Denmark is leading the way across all four categories assessed — energy use, greenhouse gas emissions, renewable energy and national climate policy. A total of 15 states, including Lithuania, Chile, and Morocco, received an overall "high" rating, which is two more than last year.

The European Union also moved up a spot, while Hungary jumped 21 places after the ousting of former prime minister Viktor Orban's government, which had repeatedly vetoed EU climate plans, dismissing them as a "utopian fantasy."

The top three positions on the CCPI remained vacant again this year, as no country has yet done enough to meet global climate goals aimed at preventing worsening weather extremes and climate damage.

"We are seeing a striking contrast," said Burck. "Progress on climate action is often slow and in some countries, such as the United States, things are even moving backwards. But technologically and economically there is enormous momentum."

That momentum is apparent in record solar energy growth. Last year 75% of global electricity demand growth was met by the green energy source, according to energy think tank Ember's latest global electricity review. Investment in clean energy has also outpaced that in fossil fuels for multiple years.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The rapid expansion of renewable technology, as well as the Iran War and a reduction in deforestation are behind a projected slight fall in emissions for the first time since the COVID-19 pandemic, according to the CCPI.

"Governments have to act now to turn the momentum into sustained emissions reductions," said CCPI co-author Niklas Höhne of the NewClimate Institute, which compiles the report with environmental NGO Germanwatch.

Burck attributed Germany's worst ever performance in the category of national climate policy to current policies being pursued by Germany's economy minister Katherina Reiche.

"Measures that primarily aim to increase the use of natural gas, threaten to undermine progress in the energy transition and risk significantly worsening the conditions for renewable energy and electrification for many years to come," said Burck.

A European Commission report published on November 9 on the sidelines of the UN COP31 climate summit in Turkey said Germany was one of nine EU countries set to miss 2030 emissions reductions targets.

Germany is not alone in its disappointing ranking. The other G20 countries — the world's leading industrialized and emerging economies, responsible for around 80% of global CO2 emissions — also perform poorly.

The only exception among them is the United Kingdom, which ranks seventh and received a high rating, performing well in greenhouse gas emissions, energy use and climate policy. However, study authors rated it low for renewable energy expansion.

The G20's oil- and gas-producing countries occupy some of the lowest positions on the climate action table. The United States, which is the world's second largest emitter, languishes alongside Russia, Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates and Canada around the bottom of the league, with an overall rating of "very low."

The hosts of this year's COP31, also received a "low" overall score. Australia, a major coal exporter with some of the world's highest per-capita emissions, ranks 54th, while Turkey, which is also heavily dependent on fossil fuels, comes in 53rd.

China is the world's largest emitter of greenhouse gases and ranks 56th in the CCPI, receiving an overall rating of "very low." Its main weaknesses include its now high per-capita emissions and substantial energy consumption.

However, among the G20, China leads the way in renewable energy expansion. The country, which is five years ahead of schedule in reaching its goal of adding 1,200 GW of wind and solar capacity to the grid by 2030, also produces over 80% of the world's solar panels.

Several oil-producing countries, including Kazakhstan, Saudi Arabia, Uzbekistan and the United Arab Emirates, are also performing better than expected in the renewables category and "are significantly expanding their previously limited" capacity, said the report.

The authors said these countries have significant potential to further expand renewables.

"In the Arab states in particular, very high per-capita emissions and an above-average level of electrification coincide with a relatively low existing share of renewable energy and enormous solar potential," said co-author Natalie Pelekh in a statement. "These are, in fact, ideal conditions for more ambitious climate action."

This article was originally published in German.

#719. John Christ, Guitarist With Danzig, Dies at 61

"He was an impressively brilliant guitarist and a wonderfully kind man," reads a tribute from Soundgarden.

John Christ, the veteran electric guitarist who wielded the axe for Danzig and Samhain and was widely recognized by the metal community as one of the best to do it, has passed away following a battle with poor health. He was 61. Explore Billboard Danzig See latest videos, charts and news

“It is with a heavy heart that we must inform you of the peaceful passing of John Christ on November 15, 2026,” reads a statement posted on Danzig’s socials. Related Underscores Is First Transgender Woman Nominated for Best Dance/Electronic Recording Grammy Ella Langley Becomes First Act to Earn Top Two of TouchTunes Frontline Chart El Coyote Earns Third Regional Mexican Airplay No. 1 With 'Ranchero Enamorado'

Born John Wolfgang Knoll, in Baltimore, Maryland, the youngest and only boy of five kids, the future rocker got a relatively traditional music education, initially on the piano before picking up the acoustic guitar, and then plugged in at age 13. Both his parents were accomplished musicians.

In the late ‘80s he dropped out of college, relocated to New Jersey and joined forces with ex-Misfits frontman Glenn Danzig on the black-as-night rock band Samhain, which would later become Danzig. Christ auditioned for the spot, and caught the attention of Danzig and Rick Rubin, who was scouting acts for his record label, Def Jam Recordings, with a performance that was both brutal and bloody, thanks to strumming finger gashed on the strings.

The anecdote is retold on Christ’s biography. “Accidentally brushing up against Glenn, he left five bloody lines on his shoulder. Rubin thought this was awesome—Danzig did not agree—he thought Christ was on speed,” it reads. When he didn’t receive an immediate callback, he pushed the process by leaving guitar riffs on Danzig’s answering machine. It was the stuff Danzig couldn’t ignore.

Christ would often catch the attention with his playing, his bluesy hard-rock sound with frequent pinch harmonics earning him a spot in Guitar World’s list of “The 100 Greatest Metal Guitarists,” coming in at No. 63.

As a member of Danzig from 1987 to 1995, Christ worked on four studio albums and one EP—Danzig (1988), Danzig II: Lucifuge (1990), Danzig III: How the Gods Kill (1992), Thrall-Demonsweatlive (1993), Danzig 4P (1994), and featured on Live on the Black Hand Side (2001) and The Lost Tracks of Danzig (2007). Christ and Danzig graced the charts with “Mother,” which peaked at No. 43 on the Billboard Hot 100 in 1994, and with a string of albums. All told, 14 Danzig titles have impacted the Billboard 200, including a best of No. 24 for Danzig III: How The Gods Kill.

Christ also contributed to the recording of the final Samhain record, Final Descent, its release delayed until 1990, and he’d go on to share the stage with the likes of Metallica, Black Sabbath, Slayer, Suicidal Tendencies, Soundgarden, White Zombie, Type O Negative, Marilyn Manson, Korn, and Corrosion of Conformity.

In a post from early September, Christ revealed that he’d been focusing on a medical issue that “has been kicking my butt and I am in the process of recuperating.”

Without giving away further details, he explained he’d been advised to “take a few months off to rest up and let my body get back to normal or else they said they will send Glenn to my house to babysit—that is motivation enough to get better.”

The heavy rock and metal community is remembering Christ as a talent, and a fine person.

“Soundgarden are very saddened to learn of the passing of John Christ,” reads a statement from the band. “He was an impressively brilliant guitarist and a wonderfully kind man. John had played with Samhain and was the original guitarist for Danzig when Soundgarden was invited to join them on tour during late summer of 1990.”

#718. Chris Pratt to Star in Sci-Fi Movie ‘The Traveler’ as He Inks Paramount First-Look

The film has Zach Lipovsky and Adam Stein set to direct.

By Aaron Couch, Borys Kit November 18, 2026 4:26pm

Chris Pratt is taking a trip to Paramount. He will star in The Traveler for the studio, where he has also signed a first-look deal. The three-year producing pact could involve starring in projects as well for his Indivisible production banner.

The Traveler is based on Joseph Eckert’s novel, which was published over the summer. It’s a father-son story, about a man who is flung through time every morning at 7:52 a.m. The first jump pushes him 24 hours into the future, but every day, the jump doubles in time, meaning soon he’s hurtling years in a single day. His son, meanwhile, grows up to study quantum physics as he attempts to save his father, who has long been missing through time. Related Stories TV Gabriel Luna on How Arnold Schwarzenegger's Christmas Party Led Him to 'The Terminal List' and 'Dexter: Resurrection' TV Kids' Choice Awards: 'Spider-Man: Brand New Day,' Zendaya, Tom Holland, BTS Among 2026 Winners

Final Destination Bloodlines filmmakers Zach Lipovsky and Adam Stein are directing The Traveler from Justin Rhodes’ screenplay. The feature, one of the more original projects on the runway of any major studio, is gearing up to shoot next year.

Pratt’s first-look deal, meanwhile, also includes Miami Heat, which has a script from Brad Copeland and has Pratt starring and producing with Hutch Parker.

Pratt became an A-list star more than a decade ago with Guardians of the Galaxy, and went on to appear in multiple Avengers movies for Marvel. He also led the Jurassic World franchise from 2015-2022, grossing billions in the process. Earlier this year, he led the animated Super Mario Bros. Galaxy movie, which grossed $1 billion globally, and had a new season of The Terminal List out last month on Amazon.

Up next, he stars in Way of the Warrior Kid for Apple TV, which he also produced. The family opens debuts Nov. 25.

#717. NASA's Voyager 1 launched second, so how did it beat Voyager 2 to a light-day by nearly a decade?

It comes down to choices made for speed and science, as the two spacecraft flew by planets in the 1970s and 1980s.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Voyager 1 is about to reach a light-day of distance in space, but Voyager 2 won't hit the mark until about 2035. Why the big difference?

On Nov. 18, Voyager 1 will be so far away from Earth that it will take a full light-day (24 hours) to send a signal to the distant spacecraft, at 16,094,799,096 miles (25,902,068,356 kilometers). Since light is essentially the maximum speed in the universe (absent using devices like wormholes, or quantum-physics puzzles), it's a big deal — so big that NASA will be celebrating the milestone by asking fans to shine Morse Code signals at the sky.

But why will Voyager 2 take nearly a decade longer? It comes down to choices made for speed and science during the twin missions' nearly 50-year journey, specifically during the first bit when they were flying by planets. The result is Voyager 1 is zooming out at a speed of 3.5 Earth-sun distances (astronomical units a year), while Voyager 2 has a more stately speed of 3.1 Earth-sun distances, according to NASA.

The original aim of both the spacecraft, which launched about two weeks apart in 1977 with Voyager 2 going first, was to look at Jupiter and Saturn. If funding persisted, which it did, the hope was to bring Voyager 2 past Uranus and Neptune, taking advantage of a rare planetary alignment. Voyager 1, by contrast, made a turn at Saturn to look at the planet's rings and the prebiotic (pre-life-chemistry) moon of Titan, before flying outside the plane of the solar system.

NASA had a range of trajectory options to consider when launching the spacecraft, and elected to bring Voyager 1 at a faster trajectory — as illustrated in this video by Britannica, where you can quickly see the spacecraft overtaking Voyager 2 on its way to Jupiter even though Voyager 1. Voyager 1 arrived at Jupiter on March 5, 1979 while Voyager 2 got there four months later on July 9.

Each of the spacecraft then performed a "gravity assist"—a sort of slingshot around the planet in which they took a tiny bit of momentum from Jupiter to gain speed as the spacecraft flew to Saturn. This technique is used constantly, such as recently when the ESCAPADE Mars mission flew two spacecraft by Earth on the way to the Red Planet, as it allows spacecraft to gain speed while saving on fuel. The planets themselves don't slow down that much.

"Because the planet is so much more massive than the spacecraft, the transfer doesn't affect the planet to any measurable extent, but to the spacecraft it's a big deal," the Planetary Society wrote. "For example, we can calculate that during the Voyager encounters with Jupiter in 1979, Jupiter slowed down by roughly 10 to the -24th power kilometers per second — a change much too small to measure."

"But each Voyager gained about 10 km/s [6.2 miles/s], a pretty big number," the society continued about the Jupiter encounter. This was "enough to put them on a fast path to Saturn — and in the case of Voyager 2, to Uranus and Neptune as well — and eventual escape from the solar system."

With each flyby, the two spacecraft picked up speed with a single exception — during Voyager 2's encounter of Neptune. That's because the spacecraft made a turn to fly by Triton. The maneuver brought Voyager 2 over Neptune's north pole, before it turned and then was directed to begin "plunging down, out of the plane of the solar system," losing speed along the way.

Voyager 2, in fact, did not have enough speed to leave the solar system until it flew by Jupiter. "It gained about 10 km/s at Jupiter, about 5 km/s at Saturn, about 2 km/s at Uranus, and lost about 2 km/s at Neptune," the Planetary Society wrote of the speeds, which are 6.21 miles/s, 3.11 miles/s, 1.24 miles/s and a loss of 1.24 miles/s, respectively.

At any rate, these fast speeds allowed both spacecraft not only to go fast, but to eventually reach interstellar space in 2012 (Voyager 1) and 2018 (Voyager 2), respectively. With the light-day milestone now reached by Voyager 1, it is anticipated the spacecraft could work into the 2030s, as long as their nuclear power sources can last.

NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory, which manages the mission, has been carefully turning off instruments as required, and recently did a "Big Bang" procedure on both spacecraft to redistribute power supplies as best as possible. The idea is to maximize science return on both spacecraft, the only interstellar messengers we have, for as long as possible.

Elizabeth Howell (she/her), Ph.D., was a staff writer in the spaceflight channel between 2022 and 2024 specializing in Canadian space news. She was contributing writer for Space.com for 10 years from 2012 to 2024. Elizabeth's reporting includes multiple exclusives with the White House, leading world coverage about a lost-and-found space tomato on the International Space Station, witnessing five human spaceflight launches on two continents, flying parabolic, working inside a spacesuit, and participating in a simulated Mars mission. Her latest book, "Why Am I Taller?" (ECW Press, 2022) is co-written with astronaut Dave Williams.

#716. 2026 CMA Awards Performances, Ranked

As Ella Langley dominated the CMA Awards' winners circle, Billboard looks at the night's performances.

The night belonged to Ella Langley at Wednesday evening’s (Nov. 18) CMA Awards. Propelled by the success of “Choosin’ Texas,” her album Dandelion and a headlining tour, Langley won her first entertainer of the year honor. She also won female vocalist of the year, single, song and music video of the year (all for “Choosin’ Texas”) and picked up album of the year, for Dandelion.

“I have watched these awards since I was a little kid, and the award I cared most about was song of the year and entertainer of the year,” Langley said in accepting the CMA entertainer of the year honor, adding, “[there] hasn’t been a song on the radio or in my ears at all where I wasn’t imagining what that song would sound like in front of a crowd…”

Other winners during the night included Chris Stapleton, Stephen Wilson Jr., Brooks & Dunn, The Red Clay Strays and the song “McArthur,” from HARDY, Morgan Wallen, Eric Church and Tim McGraw. Lainey Wilson, hosting for a third time, opened the show by paying tribute to the late music legend Dolly Parton.

“Dolly gave us hope, Dolly gave us joy, Dolly gave us her heart,” Wilson said.

Wilson was joined at times to host by Luke Bryan, and also Brad Paisley, in a throwback to the decade-plus that Paisley and Carrie Underwood hosted the CMAs. From there, the evening celebrated the CMA Awards’ six decades of helping to showcase artists on one of country music’s biggest stages.

The evening both celebrated newcomers and established artists, while honoring legendary artists, such as attendees Sammy Kershaw, Randy Travis, Clint Black and Bill Anderson. While Langley dominated the awards wins, the night was filled with an array of performances. Taylor Swift made her first CMA Awards performance in 13 years, and turned it into an entertaining spectacle. Langley performed twice (including a collab with Miranda Lambert), while Wilson Jr. teamed with Chris Stapleton, Zach Top welcomed Dierks Bentley to pay tribute to John Anderson, and more artists shone during their time in CMA Awards spotlight.

The evening was filled with top-notch performances, including heartfelt tributes, unique artist pairings, rollicking new song debuts and of course, a few surprises.

Below, Billboard ranks each CMA Awards performance, counting down to the most memorable performance of the evening.

The CMAs aimed to honor Willie Nelson lifetime achievement award recipients Brooks & Dunn with a star-studded performance. After all, the duo has amassed a catalog of influential, enduring country hits like “Red Dirt Road,” “Boot Scootin’ Boogie,” and “Brand New Man,” and are previous CMA entertainer of the year winners, and Country Music Hall of Fame members.  But the multi-artist tribute performance was one of the weakest of the night. Right from the start, those country songs were infused with an unnecessary hard-rock vibe with Halestorm’s version of “Boot Scootin’ Boogie,” and that vibe flowed throughout much of the performance, such as HARDY’s rendition of “Hillbilly Deluxe.” Brothers Osborne, blues-rocker Marcus King, Brad Paisley and Luke Bryan were also part of the tribute, but overall, it just didn’t quite match up to other B&D tribute performances we’ve seen over the years.

Mumford & Sons and Chris Stapleton teamed up for a rendition of their collaboration “Here,” turning in a pleasant and crowd-pleasing performance, even if it wasn’t a standout of the evening.

More than three decades after earning a career-defining hit with “Don’t Take The Girl,” newly-minted Country Music Hall of Fame member Tim McGraw offered his first CMA Awards performance of the song. Seated on a stool, and donning a suit and his signature black cowboy hat, McGraw conveyed the song’s tender, heartbreaking story with a sincere, if slightly too rugged at times, vocal delivery and highlighting the song’s timeless message.

Moroney was nominated for two trophies at the CMA Awards, including song of the year for her song “Beautiful Things.” She brought that tender ballad to the CMAs stage, performing in the middle of the crowd, while seated on a flower-covered window pane setting that rose over the audience during the song, as she does in her headlining concerts. A sweet performance of a heartfelt song.

Vocal group of the year winners The Red Clay Strays turned in a soulful performance of “Revival” from their album Grateful. Lead singer Brandon Coleman’s voice as powerful as usual, while the rest of the group supported his vocals with a refined, jamband vibe.

Texas-born, powerhouse singer-songwriters Kacey Musgraves and Miranda Lambert teamed up to perform “Horses & Divorces,” a pointed track about letting bygones be bygones (from Musgraves’ Middle of Nowhere album). This track simmers with both wit and vulnerability, and their honest deliveries are undeniable. At one point, Musgraves and Lambert shared a shot during the stone-cold country track, sharing a hug as the song concluded.

Luke Combs has become one of country music’s most consistent vocalists and performers, and his CMAs performance was no exception. Donning his signature black shirt and baseball cap, he performed “Miss You Here,” from his album The Way I Am, which earned a nomination for the CMA’s album of the year. His vocals were top-notch and his band was tight-knit, delivering the high-caliber style of performance he’s known for.

Vince Gill opened the show by singing a heartfelt, piano-backed rendition of “I Will Always Love You” to honor late music icon Dolly Parton. He was then joined by Wilson, with Gill adding harmony. Straightforward and very touching, the moment made for a special tribute to the beloved Parton.

Stephen Wilson Jr. and Chris Stapleton teamed up on “I’m A Song,” a look at the power of music in shaping and sustaining memorable moments. Both Wilson Jr. and Stapleton have powerful voices, making for a distinctive vocal pairing.

Ella Langley led the CMA nominations this year with nine nominations and made her way to the winner’s circle many times during the evening. She also turned in one of the evening’s top performances with the fan-favorite “Loving Life Again.” The set was outfitted to look like a dreamy, dusky field, while Langley was accompanied by strings, lending more depth to the song’s peaceful, hopeful feel.

In addition to hosting the CMAs, Wilson debuted new music, with “Just a Woman.” Wilson is known for strong-willed anthems such as “Heart Like A Truck” and “Wild Flowers and Wildhorses,” but this performance marked one of her most soulful, passionate ballads yet. Donning a flowing dress and her signature hat, the newlywed Wilson sang of romantic, passionate and complex love and delivered a soaring vocal that reminded everyone just why she’s a multiple CMA entertainer of the year winner.

Zach Top used his CMA Awards performance to introduce a new song, “Moonshine.” The rollicking track was filled with his signature sizzling guitar licks and retro country flair. The set leaned into the song’s “barn burner” pace, as the massive screen behind Top shone with images of a barn ablaze. Then, he welcomed Dierks Bentley for a tribute to the late country singer John Anderson, with a rendition of Anderson’s 1983 hit “Swingin’.”

Miranda Lambert and Ella Langley each performed twice on the CMAs, this time teaming up with one another for the premiere performance of their collab “Snakeskin Boots,” featured on Lambert’s Crisco album. The two were clearly having fun during their playful, sultry performance and the groovy energy was palpable.

Tucker Wetmore took the show’s energy to a new level, backed by a horn section as he grooved and commanded the stage for a performance of his own song “Who Told You That.” Then, he settled in (momentarily) at a piano and delved into a cover of Hank Williams Jr.’s “All My Rowdy Friends Are Coming Over Tonight.” He brought a Jerry Lee Lewis-style energy as he kicked the piano seat away and pounded the keys, as a ring of fire surrounded him and lit up the piano, too. He far and away turned in one of the evening’s most energetic, memorable performances, showcasing a star-making sense of showmanship.

Thirteen years after her previous CMA Awards performance, one of the world’s biggest music stars returned to her country roots, as Taylor Swift performed “I Knew It, I Knew You” (from Toy Story 5). Her effervescent performance began with Swift walking through the CMA’s backstage area, and greeting artists including Lainey Wilson, Eric Church, Little Big Town and Brad Paisley along the way, before Bill Anderson handed Swift her guitar and she made her way to center stage. Swift’s always entertaining, fun and theatrical approach to performing was a perfect fit for the song, as both the staging and her outfit paid homage to the movie. Again nodding to her country music roots, she dipped into her country catalog by performing “Our Song” (which she performed on the CMA Awards stage in 2007) before returning to “I Knew It, I Knew You,” backed by guitars and horns, making it the most charismatic, memorable performance of the night.

#715. SkyShowtime to Shut Down, CEO Exiting

The writing was on the wall for the joint venture first unveiled five years ago by Comcast and the then-named ViacomCBS.

Two months after signaling that a major pull-the-plug move was going to be made, Comcast and Skydance are formally shuttering their European streaming joint venture that had been first unveiled five years ago in a far different landscape.

SkyShowtime, the service that serves more than 20 countries, will wind down at the end of 2027, the board of directors for the company informed staff on Wednesday. As part of the decision, CEO Monty Sarhan will exit the streamer.

The company was unveiled in 2021 by Comcast and the then-named ViacomCBS, which had just been merged by Shari Redstone before the company rebranded as Paramount Global. It had been envisioned as a broad general entertainment streaming vehicle with 10,000-plus hours of programming housing Showtime, Nickelodeon, Paramount Pictures, Paramount+ Originals, Sky Studios, Universal Pictures and Peacock content overseas.

In June, Comcast co-CEOs Brian Roberts and Mike Cavanagh revealed a plan to split into two independent companies, cleaving off its NBCUniversal and Sky content division from its connectivity business. That spin is set to close next year and will reverberate across the entertainment landscape as NBCUniversal goes it alone (“Will it be a buyer or a seller?” questions will only grow louder).

Meanwhile, ViacomCBS morphed into Paramount Global and then was married to Warner Bros. Discovery under the banner of David Ellison’s Skydance. Showtime, which had once been a blue-chip rival to HBO, now is a name that isn’t even on the list of Skydance’s dozens of brands in its giant portfolio of cable channels, studios and streaming services.

The full memo from the board of SkyShowtime is below:

Dear SkyShowtime Employees, In September, we shared that SkyShowtime’s shareholders had initiated a review of strategic options, followed by the start of employee consultations in October. That review has now concluded, and the shareholders have made the decision to wind down SkyShowtime’s operations in late 2027. Since SkyShowtime’s launch, the streaming landscape has evolved significantly. Major global platforms have continued to expand their scale and invest heavily in content, technology, and sport. These competitive dynamics have made it increasingly challenging for regional players like SkyShowtime to achieve the scale needed for long-term success. Despite the excellent work and dedication of this team, the shareholders have determined that winding down the business is the most appropriate path forward. After over four years leading the SkyShowtime business, Monty Sarhan has agreed with the Board that it is an appropriate time to exit the company. We thank Monty for his commitment and contributions to SkyShowtime’s journey. We are also grateful to Mark Neil, who has agreed to serve as Interim General Manager, overseeing the wind-down operating period. We are committed to supporting everyone at SkyShowtime throughout this process and sharing information as decisions are implemented. In the meantime, SkyShowtime continues to operate as normal for our members. Employee consultations remain ongoing in accordance with local requirements, and timing and process may vary by country. We want to thank each of you for your hard work, professionalism, and commitment to SkyShowtime and its members. We are grateful for your contributions and will keep you informed as we move forward. The SkyShowtime Board

#714. DW Science explainer on the default mode network: what your brain does when you aren't focusing on anything, and why it's important.

Doing nothing might be the ultimate brain hack. When you're bored, the brain goes into default mode network. It's not only healthy for you, but it may also shape the very essence of your identity.

You know when you lock your phone and the screen goes black? It seems like it's not doing anything. But it's not doing nothing. It's syncing your messages, updating apps and running other background processes.

Imagine you're sitting on a bus, staring out of a window, taking a shower or walking, and you get that feeling of doing nothing and letting your mind drift?

Well, your mind, the brain, is doing a lot when it feels like you're doing nothing.

It's going over your memories, shaping your sense of who you are, imagining possible futures, helping you understand other people and connecting ideas.

That's your brain's default mode network.

Scientists conducted brain-imaging experiments in the 1990s and early 2000s to find out which regions of the brain were active during demanding tasks, like solving a math problem or memory exercise.

But to measure that, they needed a so-called baseline. They needed to know the level of brain activity at rest and during demanding tasks.

So, between the tasks, they asked participants to relax, close their eyes, stare at a fixed point on a wall, or try not to think of anything at all.

And they measured the participants' brain activity both when they were solving a task and doing nothing. That's how scientists noticed the brain was active in up- and downtime.

They noticed that when participants started to focus on a new task, after having done nothing, some brain areas lit up and other areas dimmed down. That suggests those areas that dimmed down must have been active while the participant was apparently — physically and mentally — at rest.

This realization eventually led to the discovery of the default mode network or DMN.

The DMN is crucial because it helps your brain make sense of your life and experiences.

It helps you connect and revisit memories, reflect on who you are, imagine what might happen in future scenarios, understand other people, build meaning from experience, and connect ideas in new ways.

It turns all your memories, experiences, knowledge, emotions and social information into your internal story. Think of that story as a constantly evolving, updated model of who you are and how you engage with the world around you.

But it's important to understand the DMN involves more than one area of the brain. It is a group of brain regions that light up when you're not focused on an external task.

There's another player in your brain that acts as a monitoring system. You can think of it as constantly asking "Is there anything that needs my attention?"

Imagine you're daydreaming while driving, and a car suddenly swerves into your lane.

In a fraction of a second, your daydream disappears and your attention snaps back to the road. That player is called the salience network, or SN.

The salience network helps you notice important signals, like a sound, a mistake, pain, an emotion, a threat, or something happening in your body, and helps shift the brain toward attention and control systems when action is needed.

The DMN, SN and attention/control systems constantly interact.

And the DMN doesn't just turn off completely with every hard task. Parts of it can also contribute when tasks involve memory, stories, meaning or other people.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Smartphones have filled many of the small empty moments of our days — waiting for the bus, standing in line, eating alone, lying on the couch. We are constantly looking at our devices.

So, it seems reasonable to ask: are we crowding out those moments of boredom where DMN kicks in?

Maybe. But so far, there's no strong evidence that scrolling directly affects mental health by reducing DMN time.

What we do know is that problematic smartphone use can increase stress, anxiety, task-switching and disrupt sleep.

And sleep loss and stress also have clearer evidence for altering DMN-related brain connectivity.

When your mind wanders, it might produce a great new idea.

But it might also replay an embarrassing thing you did five years ago. Again. And again.

In depression, the self-reflection part of the DMN can get caught in repetitive negative loops that are hard to stop — what's known as rumination.

Scientists have also found that Alzheimer's disease targets key DMN areas, particularly those responsible for your autobiographical memory and remembering other aspects of the past. Which may help explain why memory problems are so central to the disease.

Protect your sleep and take stress seriously. There is direct evidence that sleep loss and stress disrupt DMN-related connectivity.

Take real, quiet breaks after mentally demanding tasks, like studying. It can even help you memorize facts for your exam.

Try to reframe boredom as this essential, energy-intensive active work in your brain that builds your internal narrative and sense of self, consolidates memories, creates connections and sparks creativity.

Try waiting in line without checking your phone. Look out the window next time you take the bus or take a walk without listening to anything.

You can also try scheduling DMN time. It may be the closest thing to a real brain hack.

#713. Taylor Swift & Jack Antonoff, Ludwig Göransson Win at 2026 Hollywood Music in Media Awards: Full Winners List

And so the long march to the Oscars begins.

Taylor Swift and Jack Antonoff and Ludwig Göransson began their long march to widely predicted Oscar glory on Wednesday, Nov. 18 when the 17th annual Hollywood Music in Media Awards (HMMA) were presented at the Avalon in Hollywood, Calif.

“I Knew It, I Knew You,’’ which Swift and Antonoff wrote for Toy Story 5, won song – animated film. Swift accepted her first HMMA in a prerecorded video shown during the ceremony. (Swift was in Nashville on the same night, set to perform on the CMA Awards, where “I Knew It, I Knew You” was nominated for single of the year.)

Göransson’s score for The Odyssey won score – feature film. Last year, Göransson won two HMMAs for his work on Sinners and went on to win both the Oscar and Golden Globe for best original score.This wasGöransson’s eighth HMMA; his second in this category.

Legendary songwriter Diane Warren won her third HMMA for “One Right Here” from Maserati: The Brothers. She performed the song during the show joined by Tia Simon and Joshua Wentz. “One Right Here” was recorded by Andrea Bocelli and Jennifer Hudson for the upcoming film.

Lana Del Rey and David Arnold won song – video game (console & PC) for “First Light” from 007 First Light, which they co-wrote and Del Rey performed.

The Rise of the Red Hot Chili Peppers: Our Brother, Hillel, directed by Ben Feldman, won music documentary – special program.

Linda Perry performed her song “What Lies With You” from Linda Perry: Let It Die Here and won for song – documentary film. The Decemberists frontman Colin Meloy performed his nominated song “The Better Part of Bravery” from Wildwood, and Brother Verses Brother stars Ethan Gold and Ari Gold performed their nominated song “Brothers Keep Goin’ Anyway” from the film.

The Isley Brothers, joined by David Kushner and Pink Beard, opened the ceremony with a performance of Warren’s song “By Any Means” from the film of the same name. The video for “By Any Means,” directed by Fran Strine, won the HMMA for music video.

Michael star Jaafar Jackson won his first HMMA for song – onscreen performance (film) for “Bad.” Daveed Diggs won song – onscreen performance – TV show/limited series for “Raise Him Up” from The Boys, which he co-wrote with composer Christopher Lennertz.

La Bola Negra composer Raül Refree won for both score – independent film and song – independent film for “La Nieve.” The song was co-written by Guitarricadelafuente, Raül Refree, and Lucas Duran, and performed by Guitarricadelafuente.

Behemoth! won music-themed film, biopic or musical, and its director Tony Gilroy was honored for his commitment to the art of film music in Los Angeles.

The award for score – short film [live action]) went to The Seventh Turn composer Michael Wandmacher, who transformed Evanescence frontwoman Amy Lee‘s voice into a full multi-instrumental film score.

Assassin’s Creed Black Flag Resynced received two HMMAs. Composers Brian Tyler and Stephen Lukach won score – video game (console & PC), and Ubisoft Music won soundtrack album.

#712. How to make AI data centres more sustainable

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

AI companies must engage with those who oppose the expansion of data centres.Credit: Michael M. Santiago/Getty

Around the world, people are demanding a halt to the proliferation of data centres — racks of computers, housed in warehouses, that are powering the boom in artificial intelligence. Communities worry that existing infrastructure will not be able to handle the surge in demand for electricity and water, and that data centres’ energy demands will cause environmental and health problems, including increases in air pollution and greenhouse-gas emissions. The question of whether AI is going to stall climate action is explored in the first of a three-part Nature Podcast (Nature https://doi.org/rzqs; 2026).

Is the climate totally cooked? What the data say

Is the climate totally cooked? What the data say

People have many concerns about the way AI is being developed, including how it might affect safety, security and jobs. Where energy is concerned, however, any added demand for computing power can, and must, be met in smart, sustainable ways, not by burning more fossil fuels. Achieving this will take some creative thinking, and researchers need to be closely involved. Many argue that there are alternatives to relying on energy-intensive data centres, such as AI models that can run on individual computers or institutional servers, thereby consuming much less power than those run using cloud services. Efforts to develop such options need to be better funded.

Future projections of data centres’ energy demands are hard to make, because they are based on assumptions that could change. If current global trends continue, electricity consumption by data centres will go on rising. Between 2017 and 2024, it grew by around 12% per year. Figures for 2024 from the International Energy Agency (IEA), based in Paris, show most of this demand coming from three regions: the United States (45%), China (25%) and Europe (15%).

The Electric Power Research Institute, a non-profit organization in Palo Alto, California, has projected that the continued growth of US data centres could add up to 94 gigawatts of demand by 2030, equivalent to 17% of the country’s electricity consumption. Data centres currently consume more than 1.5% of the world’s electricity supply, and the IEA’s projections indicate that this figure will more than double in the next few years. By 2030, data centres could consume more electricity than Japan, the agency says.

Why scientists should lead the shift away from AI mega data centres

Why scientists should lead the shift away from AI mega data centres

There are serious concerns that this extra demand will be powered mainly by fossil fuels, when carbon emissions are already at a record high. Research published this week in Nature Sustainability estimates that some 400 data centres in the United States accounted for around 26 megatonnes of carbon dioxide emissions between May 2024 and April 2025, more than those produced by many countries (G. Guidi et al. Nature Sustain. https://doi.org/hcsptc; 2026). And according to a study published last week in Nature Climate Change, data centres’ energy demands could prolong the lifespan of coal-fired power stations (C. Li et al. Nature Clim. Change https://doi.org/rzqr; 2026).

But none of this is inevitable. Governments could mandate that new energy demand be met with renewable sources. And regulators could look at alternative ways to manage existing electric supplies.

Many nations’ electric grid systems are designed to accommodate surges in demand, whether to power extra cooling on hot summer days or extra heating during winter cold snaps. Much of the time, there is excess capacity. This excess could be used to reduce the amount of new energy needed to power data centres.

How much energy will AI really consume? The good, the bad and the unknown

How much energy will AI really consume? The good, the bad and the unknown

One solution is to curtail data-centre operations during periods of peak electricity consumption, and ramp up at times of lower demand. An analysis released in 2025 by researchers at Duke University in Durham, North Carolina, found that the US electric grid could accommodate 98 gigawatts of extra demand in this way, without adding any new generation capacity (see go.nature.com/4cdeknm). That 98 gigawatts would be enough to cover most, if not all, of the expected expansion in US data centres over the next few years.

There is potential for this to become a reality. In June, as part of a larger effort to modernize the grid, the US Federal Energy Regulatory Commission instructed grid operators to draw up a plan for how they will cope with extra demand from data centres. The technology industry is understandably paying close attention to how it might mitigate the problems of powering data centres. Earlier this month, OpenAI announced what it is calling a “grid protectors program”, a project to consult with US grid operators, regulators and policymakers to see how the company can work around peaks in power demand.

Meanwhile, Google is paying households and businesses in parts of the Eastern United States to reduce their electricity consumption during periods of high demand. Similar proposals are being considered in other countries.

Why open-source generative AI models are an ethical way forward for science

Why open-source generative AI models are an ethical way forward for science

These are all tentative moves in the right direction, although arguably progress is not being made fast enough. Policymakers and data-centre operators must engage seriously with those who oppose the centres’ expansion. At a minimum, any new energy sources developed to power these centres must be renewable. Existing energy sources can also be better deployed, and researchers working to develop alternatives to energy-intensive data centres should be better supported. More peer-reviewed evidence is needed, especially for countries outside the United States.

There are smarter and more sustainable ways to power the growth of AI, but to achieve them, concerted and coordinated action will be needed. In this way, the harm posed to people and the planet can be minimized, and AI technologies can benefit everyone.

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03708-6

#711. Rob Lowe Asked Ben Shapiro to Cast Him in ‘Confession’: “I’ve Worked With Left-Wing Writers. Why Wouldn’t I Work With Right-Wing Writers?”

The Daily Wire founder recently said he told the actor he was "way too handsome" to take on the role.

Rob Lowe was ready to sign on to star in Ben Shapiro‘s Confession after he read the “fantastic” script written by the Daily Wire founder.

The Emmy nominee went on the Second Thought podcast Tuesday, where he recounted how he got involved with the film. He started, “I read the script; it was written by Ben Shapiro. I called Ben and said, ‘This is fantastic.’ And he was like, ‘Well, do you think you know anybody 50-ish, leading man who would not be scared just because I wrote it?’ And I go, ‘Yeah, me.’”

“And he goes, ‘You’re good with this?’ I said, ‘I’ve worked with the most left-wing writers in the world. Why wouldn’t I also work with the most right-wing writers in the world?’” Lowe added. Related Stories Movies 'Confession' Review: Rob Lowe and James Franco in a Ben Shapiro-Scripted, Stalinist Russia-Set Drama That's Terminally Tedious Midterms 2026 Ben Shapiro Says 2026 Midterms Were "A Wipeout for Republicans": "The President Was Kind of on the Ballot"

During a recent appearance on the Conversations With Coleman podcast on Saturday, Shapiro said that the actor called him and said he was “deeply affected by the script.” When he asked if he could play the lead part, Shapiro said he replied by saying, “You’re Rob Lowe. If you ask to play a part, the answer is yes, but I’m just telling you you’re way too handsome for this. Like, you’re way too good-looking for this part.”

Of Confession, Lowe said the movie was “turned down by every single film festival.” He added, “Summarily frog-marched out of any conversation. Now, this is a movie with me, Nick Nolte, James Franco, Emile Hirsch. I see what they’re picking up, and it’s all political.”

“The thought would be we’d play in a film festival, we would get some buzz, never happened. And then you know Netflix would pick it up or this one would pick — crickets. Absolute crickets,” Lowe said. “So then it defaults to the Daily Wire to be the distributor, and I’m like, hell yeah. I want people to see this movie. And good for them for putting it out. But that wasn’t originally going to be the life of the movie.”

Confession was directed by Václav Marhoul and centers on the interrogation of a prisoner in a Stalin-era Russian jail.

#710. 1 light-day from Earth! NASA's Voyager 1 probe hits huge milestone in interstellar space
